items.title: From Atiku’s spokesmen to Tinubu’s spokesmen – yesterday, Atiku; today, Tinubu; tomorrow, who knows?, by Stephanie Shaakaa
items.description: A microphone has no permanent owner. The man holding it today may well be holding it for somebody else tomorrow. Segun Showunmi has given Nigerians another reason to examine the curious business of political loyalty. Read Also: 2027: Atiku suffering from ‘Emir complex’ — Segun Sowunmi On October 15, 2026, he urged the public to support President Bola Tinubu’s re-election, declaring that prosperity is around the corner. He is now part of Tinubu’s presidential campaign communications team, persuading citizens that the President deserves four more years. There is a detail worth remembering. Showunmi was the spokesman for Atiku Abubakar’s presidential campaign in 2019. Daniel Bwala, who served as a spokesman for Atiku’s 2023 campaign, is now Tinubu’s Special Adviser on Media and Public Communication. If Nigerian politics were a church, these two would have explaining to do about their conversion. One can almost see the congregation watching as yesterday’s defenders of one ambition arrive to preach the merits of another. The faces are familiar. The voices have not changed. Only the object of their praise has. Showunmi and Bwala are free to change their minds. Nobody owns another man’s political allegiance forever. They can leave a party, embrace a former opponent, and discover fresh reasons to support a politician they once challenged. That is their constitutional right. But there is a vast difference between changing your mind and expecting the public to develop amnesia. These men were not casual supporters arguing politics over drinks. They were campaign spokesmen. They stood before cameras, spoke to journalists, defended their principals, and tried to persuade Nigerians to see presidential candidates through a specific lens. Their words were meant to shape public opinion in a contest for the highest office in the land. When Daniel Bwala declared on social media before his crossover that “The human brain is unique and miraculous… UNTIL YOU JOIN APC, THEN IT STOPS WORKING,” he was not offering a lighthearted joke. He was selling Nigerians a definitive moral assessment. Yet after joining the President’s camp, he brushed aside his past critiques during an Al Jazeera interview by insisting, “It’s all politics.” Really? If a spokesman can spend an election campaign arguing that a candidate is a threat to the nation, then cross over to that candidate’s camp and declare his former denunciations irrelevant, where does campaign duty end and personal conviction begin? Now the scenery has changed, and the public is expected to receive their new message with the same confidence with which they delivered the old one. Showunmi’s declaration that prosperity is around the corner makes the issue particularly urgent. Nigerians have spent years hearing explanations for hardship, assurances that reforms will eventually pay off, and promises that the pain of today is the price of a better tomorrow. The market woman still calculates what she can afford before buying food. The worker still watches transport fares swallow a growing share of his salary. Parents still struggle with school fees, rent, electricity bills, and the cost of keeping a household running. For millions of people, the corner called prosperity has become a destination repeatedly announced but never quite reached. Showunmi is entitled to believe Tinubu deserves another term. But he must do more than announce that better days are approaching. He should tell Nigerians what evidence supports his optimism, what tangible improvements they should already see, and when the promised relief will begin to make a difference in their lives. A campaign spokesman can sell hope; he cannot demand that hardship be mistaken for progress simply because he has found a more powerful principal. If Tinubu’s reforms are working, Showunmi should make the case. If the President’s policies have put Nigeria on a path to growth, let him explain the evidence and show how the benefits will reach ordinary households. If continuity is the answer, let him explain why citizens should endure another four years rather than choose a different direction. The microphone gives him an audience. It does not give him immunity from questions. Perhaps Bwala sincerely reconsidered his position. Perhaps Showunmi discovered genuine merit in the President’s leadership. People can change their minds for valid reasons, and we need not invent sinister motives to demand an explanation. The metaphor that clings most obstinately to this political culture remains transactional,an indictment of an establishment where political conviction lasts only as long as the arrangement remains lucrative. Welcome to the Nigerian political marketplace, where the occupants change rooms, the promises acquire fresh packaging, and yesterday’s sworn enemies discover they have always shared common ground. The cost of this arrangement is not merely the embarrassment of watching familiar faces defend unfamiliar positions. It is the steady erosion of public trust. When political arguments change with the fortunes of the people making them, citizens have reason to question whether they are hearing honest assessments of the country’s problems or simply the latest sales pitch from a campaign office. Showunmi and Bwala need not apologize for leaving Atiku’s camp. They do, however, have an opportunity to demonstrate that their present positions rest on more than the convenience of political realignment. They can explain what they believe Tinubu has done right, address what he has done wrong, and make a credible case for why another term would serve Nigeria’s interests. As 2027 approaches, the country will be crowded with people eager to explain why their preferred candidate deserves power. Some will have remained loyal to one camp for decades. Others will have traveled through several parties, alliances, and campaign offices. Voters should judge each argument on its merits, but they must not be expected to forget the history of the people making it. Nigerians are not an audience to be entertained between elections, nor are they customers obliged to buy whatever a familiar salesman places before them. They have to live with the consequences of political decisions long after campaign slogans have faded and spokesmen have moved on. Showunmi can tell Nigerians that prosperity is near. Bwala can defend the President’s record. Both men can campaign for Tinubu with all the eloquence they possess. But the public is entitled to place their present arguments beside their past ones and ask the question that neither a new title nor a new political uniform can make disappear. If you were right then, what changed? And if you are right now, why should we believe you? Asking these questions is not persecution,it is the tax every holder of a public microphone must pay. Holding men to their own recorded words is not an attack,it is the bare minimum duty of a critical electorate. The microphone may belong to whoever is holding it. The judgment belongs to the people listening. Stephanie Shaakaa shaakaastephanie@yahoo.com 08078600871 The post From Atiku’s spokesmen to Tinubu’s spokesmen – yesterday, Atiku; today, Tinubu; tomorrow, who knows?, by Stephanie Shaakaa appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: WB urges Pakistan to shift from stability to growth
items.description: WORLD Bank official Sandeep Mahajan meets Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb.—X/ @Financegovpk • Calls for stronger investment, private sector activity • Aurangzeb stresses need to strengthen investor confidence ISLAMABAD: In what appears to be a push towards accelerating growth, the World Bank has advised Pakistan to move from stabilisation to sustainable growth, with a focus on strengthening investment and private sector activity. This marks the second such endorsement from the international financial institution, which recently commended Pakistan’s stabilisation programme and urged a shift towards sustainable growth to generate employment opportunities for the youth. The IMF has also offered similar advice to Islamabad at a recent workshop on tax reforms. World Bank Regional Practice Director for the Prosperity Vertical for the Middle East, North Africa, Afghanistan and Pakistan (MENAAP) Sandeep Mahajan met Finance Minister Muhammad Aurangzeb on Friday. He was accompanied by Country Director Bolor­maa Amgaabazar and International Finance Corporation (IFC) Division Director Simon Andrews. An official statement said the meeting discussed Pakistan’s economic reform agenda, the transition from stabilisation to sustainable growth and priorities for strengthening inve­stment and private sector activity. Mr Mahajan congratulated Pakis­tan on restoring macroeconomic stability and commended the government’s management of the recent crisis arising from regional conflict. He noted that buffers built through stabilisation efforts and a timely policy response had helped Pakistan manage external pressures. World Bank representatives emphasised the importance of sustaining these gains through continued reforms and effective implementation. Mr Aurangzeb said the government’s priority was to make macroeconomic stability durable and translate it into sustainable, investment-led and export-driven growth. He said that Pakistan had regained access to international capital markets, including through its recent $3 billion Eurobond issuance with five-year and 10-year maturities. The minister also stressed the need to secure further credit rating upgrades, strengthen investor confidence and improve Pakistan’s sovereign credit profile. Mr Aurangzeb underscored the importance of a credible transition framework that maintained fiscal discipline, addressed external sector vulnerabilities and strengthened the foundations for private sector-led, responsible and sustainable growth. The discussion also covered international experience in strengthening fiscal frameworks and policy credibility to manage external risks and support investor confidence. Policy continuity was highlighted as another key requirement for sustained economic progress. The finance minister noted that investment and productivity depended on a predictable policy environment and consistent implementation. Mr Aurangzeb and the World Bank representatives also exchanged views on the government’s growth and jobs agenda, including opportunities to strengthen private sector investment, improve the regulatory environment and mobilise financing for infrastructure. The discussion covered privatisation, the importance of clear regulatory frameworks and credible post-privatisation arran­gements, as well as the potential to develop infrastructure projects through appropriate financing structures and collaboration with development partners. Both sides reaffirmed the importance of continued cooperation between Pakistan and the World Bank, with a focus on sustaining macroeconomic stability, advancing structural reforms, strengthening policy continuity and translating reform gains into investment, employment and improved economic opportunities. Published in Dawn, October 24th, 2026

items.title: Carrick refuses to rule out dropping Fernandes in emotional address
items.description: Under-pressure Manchester United boss Michael Carrick delivered a passionate and emotional address lasting five minutes and 30 seconds as he battles to save his job. And he refused to rule out dropping skipper Bruno Fernandes for Sunday’s Premier League meeting with Bournemouth at Old Trafford. Instead of taking his seat and answering questions as normal in Friday’s scheduled pre-match media conference at Carrington, Carrick said he wanted to start himself. It was a strategy former boss Sir Alex Ferguson used, although the legendary Scot rarely spoke at such length. After a run of seven games without a win, culminating in Wednesday’s shocking 4-1 Champions League defeat by Como, and attacks on the club’s hierarchy by defender Lisandro Martinez and then Fernandes’ condemnation of his own tactics in Italy, Carrick wanted to reaffirm his view of what United stood for. “Recently we haven’t had a good time, I think that’s pretty obvious,” he said. “Wednesday was a bad night, and it hurt me to see us play like that. It was unacceptable. “My responsibility is to get a team on the pitch that represents this football club, and the supporters, and they can be proud of in the identity we show. We have gone away from that recently. It’s important we all recognise that. “The foundation and values of this football club have been etched for many years. I totally understand and get every single one of them. “There’s a resilience about this football club that runs very deep. I’ve seen it with my own eyes, I’ve felt it, I’m know some of the individuals closely who have been a big part of that history. “Entitlement cannot be at this football club. “It was based on being humble, having humility, and hard work. We can never lose that, and I won’t let us lose that.” Asked about Fernandes and whether he has considered dropping him, a defiant Carrick added: “The most important thing for me is the team, the squad and dynamics in the squad. “It’s about the football club. I’ll always do what is best for the football club.” No guarantees for Fernandes Image caption,Manchester United won 12 of their 17 games under Michael Carrick last season Club sources said on Thursday Fernandes would not have the captaincy taken away or be fined for his post-match observations following the Como defeat. In a further interview on Wednesday night with Sky Italia, the Portugal international referred to Manchester United’s storied history. “At this club, there’s too much focus on what’s been done in the past,” said Fernandes. “But we’re not those people anymore. The club and the players need to understand that. “Unfortunately for us – especially when it comes to the players – those who join expect to win trophies, win games, and reach the highest level, that’s been very difficult at this club in recent years.” Whether Carrick was aware of Fernandes’ comments about United’s history before he spoke was uncertain. When asked again if he would take the captaincy away from the 32-year-old midfielder, Carrick repeated: “I will always do what is best for the football club.” He then refused to say whether he had spoken to Fernandes about his conduct, adding: “I don’t think this is the time to go into too much detail.” Despite the challenge to his authority, Carrick said the United dressing room was not divided. “No, it’s not,” he added. “We just need to get back to doing what we do best.” Carrick also said the club were ‘doing everything’ to support Fernandes and his family, whose Cheshire home was burgled on Wednesday. “Thankfully they weren’t directly affected even though it is an awful situation.” ‘Hurt’ fuels motivation and inspiration Carrick named legendary United figures such as Ryan Giggs, Wayne Rooney and Ferguson as examples of the humility, sacrifice and hard work expected of United players. That was at odds with his post-match criticism on Wednesday, when he said if you don’t run forward or back properly, you will not win games. Asked how he would persuade his current squad to adhere to the values expected and he demanded, Carrick added: “It’s clear as day. “I’m not telling you anything new. I haven’t invented that. That’s the make-up of any good football team. You have to earn the right to be better than your opponent. That never changes. “What we look like as a group is my responsibility. That’s the privileged position I am in. I’ll hold that umbrella for me to get wet and everyone else to stay dry. “[Wednesday] hurts an awful lot, but that doesn’t stop me. That hurt is used as pure motivation and inspiration to want more, expect more and get us going in a different direction.”

items.title: ‘Courts are now market stalls’: Nigerians react to Justice Augie’s jabs on judiciary
items.description: •‘If we lose courts, we lose election before first vote’ •Nigeria’s judiciary on trial — Welson •Courtroom should not be turned into final polling unit — Adewale By Dayo Johnson, Regional Editor, South West A retired justice of the Supreme Court, Justice Amina Adamu Augie, last week raised the alarm that corruption within Nigeria’s judiciary and legal profession is eroding public aconfidence in the administration of justice and transforming the courts into what she described as “market stalls.” Read Also: Nigeria’s rule of law under threat, justice too slow, costly – Ex-Supreme Court Justice, Augie Justice Augie, who spoke in Abuja during the 40th anniversary celebration of the Nigerian Law School Class of 1986, popularly known as the Centennial Class, said corrupt practices involving judges, lawyers and court officials had weakened the credibility of the justice system and damaged the public’s perception of the legal profession. It is a notorious fact that many people no longer see the judiciary as the last hope of the common people. And in a society where the residents do not have confidence in the judiciary to deliver justice, the consequences can not be imagined. Less than three months to the 2027 general elections therefore, concerned Nigerians have warned that the judiciary must not be allowed to determine the outcome of the elections. They argued that the judiciary has demonstrated times without number that it cannot be trusted and some candidates are not thinking of going to the election tribunal to retrieve any mandate but to settle the matter on the election day. If we lose the courts before February 2027, we lose the election before the first vote is cast — Prof Okaba A university don and immediate past President, Ijaw National Congress, Prof Benjamin Okaba said: “Retired Supreme Court Justice Amina Augie’s warning must be taken seriously, because an election is only as credible as the court that will judge it. Corruption will impact the 2027 elections in three ways: pre-election manipulation, election-day impunity, and post-election anarchy. When registry staff can make files disappear, delay service, or backdate affidavits, elections are rigged before ballot papers are even printed, as seen in 2023 pre-election matters where candidates were excluded through technical fraud. To tackle this, the three arms Justice Augie identified must be fixed. For the Bench, the National Judicial Council must act swiftly and publicly: no judge with a pending corruption petition should serve on any Election Petition Tribunal in 2027, and all tribunal proceedings and judgments must be live-streamed, as was piloted in 2023, sunlight is the best disinfectant. For the Bar, the Nigerian Bar Association must stop protecting senior lawyers who act as bagmen for judges; the notorious practice of “go and see the judge” must attract debarment, not promotion to SAN. For the Registry, the most neglected but most dangerous, total digitalization is needed: electronic filing with time stamps, CCTV in registries, and audit trails will end the era where a clerk can decide the fate of a governorship. Above all, speed is essential. The 180-day rule for tribunals must be sacrosanct, because the longer a petition stays in the system, the more time for market-stall bargaining. Justice Augie has sounded the alarm, and the CJN, NBA, EFCC, ICPC, and civil society must act now. If we lose the courts before February 2027, we would have lost the election before the first vote is cast.” Courtroom should not be turned into final polling unit where money casts deciding vote — Adewale On his part, former SDP chairman in Ondo state, Hon Stephen Adewale said, “Justice Augie’s warning should trouble every Nigerian as we approach the 2027 elections. If politicians believe they can purchase judicial protection, electoral malpractice becomes a calculated investment. A stolen mandate could pass through the courts and emerge wearing the robes of legitimacy. Corruption among registry officials can be equally destructive, especially where evidence is concealed or access to documents is deliberately frustrated. The damage could outlive the election. Citizens who endure long queues to vote may lose faith in democracy if they believe money will eventually determine whose victory survives. The National Judicial Council must investigate credible complaints promptly and impose meaningful sanctions where misconduct is established. “Lawyers and registry officials who facilitate corruption must also face consequences, alongside politicians who offer bribes. Secured digital records and timely access to electoral evidence would make manipulation harder. Financial independence of the judiciary must come with accountability, while honest judges must be protected from political intimidation. No politician should be allowed to turn the courtroom into a final polling unit where money casts the deciding vote. Protection of electoral justice must be treated as democratic imperative — Ogunsuyi A Public Analyst, Media Consultant and Former Commissioner for Information in Ekiti State, Lanre Ogunsuyi, said, “The credibility of Nigeria’s 2027 general elections will depend not only on the proper conduct of voting and the accurate collation of results, but also on whether electoral disputes are resolved by courts that are independent, impartial and beyond the reach of corruption. If judicial decisions can be bought, manipulated or shaped by political pressure, the election itself becomes vulnerable to illegitimacy. Compromised electoral justice would not merely damage the reputation of the courts; it could determine who governs, overturn the will of voters, and place the constitutional order under strain. When justice appears to be for sale, public confidence collapses, legitimate mandates are questioned, and aggrieved parties may abandon lawful remedies. The consequences are concrete and dangerous: defeated candidates may reject court judgments as predetermined, supporters may mobilise against institutions, and disputes that should end in the courtroom may spill into protests, violence or prolonged political instability. A system that denies citizens a credible legal remedy creates incentives for self-help and makes peaceful transfers of power far less certain. As preparations for the 2027 elections gather momentum, Nigeria must treat the protection of electoral justice as a democratic imperative. Corruption in electoral justice should be difficult to perpetrate, easier to expose and impossible to excuse once established. Democracy does not thrive merely because votes are cast and counted; it endures when citizens trust that disputes will be resolved fairly, that unlawful victories can be overturned and that justice, not influence, will determine who holds power”. Clean up judiciary to save Nigeria’s democracy — Ambakaderimo For Elder Joseph Ambakederimo, Convener South South Reawakening Group, “The retired Supreme Court Justice tried to be lenient on her colleagues at the Bench, Bar, and the Registry. The actual description for me would be like a “Bazaar” where items are being auctioned to the highest bidder. The corruption in the judicial arm of government has reached a crisis point that has become irreversible. As it is today, who will bell the cat? Who will stand in and clean the Augean stable? We can recollect vividly when the President Buhari administration tried to intervene; he couldn’t get cooperation from everyday Nigerians who hitherto bear the brunt of the endemic corruption in the country. The rhetorical question to ask is: if corruption flows from top to bottom and from bottom to top, pervading all aspects of our lives, what makes one think that one part (the judicial arm of the same government) would be immune to the malaise we suffer as a country? For me, I think it will be an uphill task to get out of this doldrums.” Candidates’ trajectory will determine outcome, Says Atare Similarly, Mr. Ufuoma Atare, the Convener, Delta Democrats Forum, DDF, said: “The trajectory of the candidates being projected by the various political parties will determine the outcome of the elections. Corruption will have minimal effect on the outcome of the 2027 elections because Nigerians are now determined to achieve proper change, just as we saw in the Osun State governorship election; people collected money and voted their conscience. The same thing will happen in 2027.” Nigerians must curtail forces derailing democracy – Uwoghiren According to lawyer and human rights activist Jefferson Uwoghiren, “Democracy thrives when people know their votes count, but when they realise their votes are likely to be ambushed or arrested, there is usually a resort to, not just violence but to anti-patriotic actions. It is therefore in the interest of this country that we all faithfully and respectfully abide by the democratic tenets we practice. Going forward, there are different agencies and institutional checks in place that are supposed to check and act. There is the Senate Committee on Judiciary, which can hold a public hearing and ask for the relevant information, knowledge and details. These are matters of public concern, and with that everybody will sit up. The media also have a role to play in checking the situation; in very advanced countries, journalists adopt very ethical means to expose these things by having what they call sting operations and then finding out who is actually going to fall for it. “Justice Augie is not a flippant person; she has seen it all. There are numerous actors responsible for these judicial blights: lawyers, judicial staff, senior government officials and wealthy and influential members of the society”. Nigeria’s judiciary on trial — Prof Welson Prof Ekiyor Welson, Executive Director Centre for Philosophy and Development said: “The judiciary has now exposed itself as an institution that cannot and should not be trusted. Because of this, we may enter a period in Nigeria that will resemble a jungle society. The opposition is determined to win the election, and any contrary result will not be accepted. Next year’s election will be decided at the polls by voters. For the first time, underrating and underestimating the opposition has become very risky. The judiciary will not be given the opportunity to take part in the election. That is the current situation. So the impact the judiciary might make, which is likely to be negative, will not arise, because nobody is thinking of going to the tribunal to retrieve any mandate. On election day, every matter will be settled.” Judiciary must purge itself, regain public trust — Morris Former Secretary, Civil Liberties Organisation (CLO) Bayelsa State, Alagoa Morris said: “The good side of this latest indictment by one who has been part of the judiciary is that the self-critique is exercised by some members of the profession. It is however sad and unfortunate that public confidence in the judiciary has been eroded, as some would boldly say that they will buy judgment. “The NBA leadership also mentioned this not too long ago. We read about the incorruptible judge once, even as children; it gave a positive feeling about the judiciary then. The judiciary should purge itself and strive to regain public confidence. If the judiciary is gone, as in a marketplace, society is finished. As one of the social institutions which strengthen developed societies, this pillar should be a strong one for Nigeria.” We must protect the ballot, defend the rule of law, restore public confidence in the administration of justice — Chief Amure Chief Ola Amure said “Corruption in the Bench, the Bar and the Court Registry poses a serious threat to Nigeria’s democracy, particularly as the country approaches the 2027 general elections. When justice becomes a commodity for sale, the consequences go beyond the courtroom. Electoral corruption can undermine the will of the people, while judicial corruption can destroy the last hope of candidates and citizens seeking redress when their electoral rights are violated. The danger is that when votes are manipulated and justice is allegedly compromised, the people may lose confidence in both the electoral process and the judiciary. This can encourage electoral violence, deepen political apathy and create a dangerous perception that elections are won not by the people’s mandate but by money, influence and connections. To tackle this menace ahead of 2027, we must strengthen the independence of the judiciary, ensure transparent and merit-based judicial appointments, investigate credible allegations of judicial corruption, and prosecute proven offenders regardless of their status. The activities of court registries must be transparent, while electoral disputes must be handled promptly, impartially and in accordance with the law. As Nigeria approaches the 2027 general elections, the preservation of judicial integrity is not merely a professional responsibility; it is a national imperative. We must protect the ballot, defend the rule of law and restore public confidence in the administration of justice. Electronic voting can curb corruption, protect election results – MBF President The National President of the Middle Belt Forum (MBF), Dr. Bitrus Pogu, on his part called for the adoption of a fully automated electoral system ahead of the 2027 general elections, saying electronic voting and real-time transmission of results would significantly reduce corruption and protect the integrity of the polls. The MBF President cautioned that the pervasive nature of corruption across public institutions posed a serious threat to credible elections if urgent measures were not taken to address it. The judiciary should not be allowed to determine the outcome of elections. Elections should be so transparent and electronically controlled using technology that if the judiciary is going to be involved in the electoral process at all, it will be to decide on disputes over who is supposed to be a legitimate candidate rather than who has won an election. Only the quality of a people can secure society’s well-being, not technology, laws, or wealth – Chief Biose Chairman of the Delta State Obidient Elders Council, Chief Chris Biose, said: “No amount of technological devices, no amount of legal provisions, no amount of money in the bank or from crude oil can ensure the well-being of a society, only the quality of the human beings in that society can. “When the quality of human beings in a society is debilitated, that society is debilitated, and there is no redemption. When you have corrupt minds in leadership, the society is doomed.” Moruff O. Balogun, former Vice Chairman, Nigerian Bar Association (NBA), Ijebu Ode Branch said; “Judicial corruption in Nigeria threatens the credibility of the 2027 general elections and undermines democracy, the rule of law, and public confidence in the judiciary. As Nigeria approaches the 2027 general elections, the integrity of the judiciary will be crucial to ensuring that electoral disputes are resolved fairly, transparently and in accordance with the law. A credible election requires more than peaceful voting and accurate collation of results; it also requires an impartial judicial system capable of protecting the mandate of the electorate. Ultimately, judicial justice must be determined by the law and evidence, not by money, political influence or intimidation. The judiciary must remain the last hope of the common man, not a marketplace where justice is available to the highest bidder. Kareem Adekola, Chairman, Nigerian Bar Association, Ibadan Branch “Corruption in the judiciary poses a serious threat to the credibility of any democratic process because elections do not end with the casting and counting of votes. There must also be confidence that disputes arising from the process will be resolved fairly, independently and strictly in accordance with the law. “If litigants believe that electoral cases can be determined by financial influence rather than evidence and the law, public confidence in the courts will suffer. It could also encourage political actors to pursue their interests through improper channels instead of respecting established democratic procedures. Ultimately, the integrity of electoral justice depends on the willingness of everyone within the justice system to defend the law above personal, financial or political interests.” According to Niyi Aborisade, a human rights lawyer; “If the judiciary fails to protect electoral justice, the consequences could extend beyond individual disputes to the legitimacy of democratic institutions. The greatest danger is that citizens may begin to believe that their votes do not matter because political power can be secured or retained through financial influence rather than popular support and the rule of law. “Such a perception could discourage voter participation, deepen political distrust and increase tensions after elections. The solution must go beyond public condemnation. The National Judicial Council and other relevant authorities must investigate credible allegations of judicial misconduct, ensure transparent disciplinary procedures and protect judges who refuse improper pressure from politicians and other influential individuals. Nigeria needs courts where evidence determines cases, not the financial strength or political connections of litigants.” Evelyn Ologbese, Civil Society and Access to Justice advocate said: “Justice must never become a privilege reserved for the wealthy, politically connected or influential members of society. “As the 2027 general elections approach, the concern is that any electoral dispute affected by improper financial influence could leave citizens feeling that their votes and constitutional rights are not adequately protected. Electoral justice must be accessible to every party, regardless of its financial resources or political standing. Urgent reforms should include transparent court procedures, digital filing and case-tracking systems, clear channels for reporting demands for bribes, and effective protection for complainants and whistle-blowers. Digitalisation alone will not eliminate corruption, but it can reduce opportunities for undocumented transactions and arbitrary administrative practices. Restoring confidence in the judiciary requires a system in which the poor and the powerful can expect the same standard of justice.” Monsurat Sunmonu, former senator representing Oyo Central and former Speaker of the Oyo State House of Assembly: “The credibility of an election depends not only on how votes are cast and counted but also on whether the institutions responsible for resolving disputes are trusted to act fairly. The judiciary has a constitutional responsibility to interpret the law without fear, favour or political interference. “Where judicial corruption is established, it can damage public confidence in electoral outcomes, regardless of which political party benefits. Democracy cannot function effectively if citizens believe that justice is determined by money or influence rather than the law. Political leaders have a responsibility to protect the independence of the judiciary, refrain from attempting to influence court proceedings and ensure that their supporters respect lawful decisions. “The 2027 elections should be an opportunity to reinforce democratic institutions, not expose them to further distrust. Ultimately, every Nigerian should be able to approach a court with the confidence that the law will be applied fairly, irrespective of political affiliation, wealth or status.” Samuel Oyadongha; Rotimi Ojomoyela; Peter Duru; Ozioruva Aliu; Daniel Abia; Ochuko Akuopha; James Ogunnaik; Emem Idio & Adeola Badru , also contributed to this report. items.title: Fuel dealers urge consumers to avoid ‘panic buying’
items.description: • PPDA chairman says pricing remains an issue • JI demands meeting with PM ‘this week’ to resolve levy issue ISLAMABAD: Even as talks between the Jamaat-i-Islami (JI) and the government to reduce the fuel levy remained ‘inconclusive’, petroleum dealers on Friday urged consumers not to resort to panic buying, as excessive purchases could create market distortions. Talking to reporters, Pakistan Petroleum Dealers Association (PPDA) Chairman Malik Khuda Baksh said the delicate balance between supply and demand had been maintained efficiently by all stakeholders, including the government, industry and consumers. At the same time, he said the recent closure of the Iran border had put the liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) market under stress. “As far as petrol supply is concerned, there is a huge responsibility on consumers too, especially petrol consumers. We have seen in the past that when cars and motorcycles line up at petrol pumps, it creates artificial shortages in some areas,” the PPDA chairman said. He said reports were circulating that the country could run dry in the coming days and recalled the situation during the US invasion of Afghanistan in October 2001. “There were such reports and a brief panic in those days too, but petrol and diesel remained available in the country. Similarly, the situation remains under control now as well,” he added. Mr Baksh said refineries were operational, while both crude oil and petroleum products were being imported from Gulf countries, including Saudi Arabia and Oman. “Price remains an issue, but that is a different matter,” he said. According to oil industry estimates, diesel demand during November 2026 is likely to be around 750,000 tonnes, driven by seasonal agricultural requirements. Industry sources said local refineries supplied approximately 70 per cent of the country’s diesel requirements, although the bulk of the crude oil processed by them was imported. Petrol demand for November is estimated at around 630,000 tonnes, while local production accounts for roughly 30pc of national consumption. Petroleum industry sources added that high prices and the off-peak travel season were likely to keep consumption subdued next month. Jamaat-govt talks Meanwhile, the JI called on Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif to announce additional relief for the public in his proposed meeting with Hafiz Naeem, and asked that the meeting be held ‘this week’. Speaking to reporters after holding talks with a government delegation led by Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal, JI Deputy Emir Liaqat Baloch told reporters that while the party would continue to pursue negotiations, it would not abandon the path of protest. As talks continue a technical committee comprising State Minister for Finance Bilal Azhar Kayani, JI Islamabad Emir Nasrullah Randhawa and Deputy Secretary Syed Farasat Shah has been constituted and the committee would meet within two to three days to examine the outstanding issues. Published in Dawn, October 24th, 2026

items.title: Ebola vaccine trial begins in DR Congo
items.description: The first clinical trial of an Ebola vaccine in the outbreak gripping the Democratic Republic of Congo began Friday, the head of the World Health Organization said. Read Also: Return of Ebola: Triumph of 2014, test of 2026 The DR Congo’s worst-ever Ebola outbreak has passed the 9,700-case mark, with the number of deaths exceeding 4,600. Among the many challenges facing the response is the lack of any approved vaccines or treatments for the Bundibugyo species of Ebola behind the epidemic. Ervebo, a vaccine approved for use against the more common Zaire strain of Ebola, will be put through a full-scale human trial in the DRC to see if it offers any cross-protection against Bundibugyo. The trial began with the first shot of Ervebo being administered in Bunia, the capital of the DRC’s northeastern Ituri province, which is the epicentre of the outbreak. “Science gives us hope. Today, in Bunia DRC, the first participants were vaccinated in a new Ebola vaccine trial called Tumaini, which means ‘hope’ in Swahili,” WHO chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on X. “This trial will help us understand whether any of the vaccine candidates designed for Bundibugyo virus work,” he said, adding that in the meantime, the existing Ervebo vaccine would be tested. “WHO is supporting this DRC-led effort to find answers and save lives.” Two vaccines in the pipeline The so-called Tumaini trial is a single trial framework that can test the safety, efficacy and immunogenicity of multiple vaccines. The trial will use a ring vaccination approach: immunising contacts deemed to be at high risk of infection. It is gearing up to incorporate two Bundibugyo-specific candidate vaccines, which are currently advancing through earlier-stage, smaller-scale clinical trials. One is a ChAdOx1 adenoviral vector jab being developed by the University of Oxford; the other, by the US-based Moderna group, uses mRNA technology. Both have received funding from the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations, and are expected to enter the trial “shortly”, CEPI said in a statement. “Tumaini will work closely with affected communities, health authorities and outbreak response partners to generate robust evidence on vaccine performance that could contribute to curtailing the epidemic, saving lives, and strengthening preparedness for future Bundibugyo outbreaks,” said CEPI. The trial will include pregnant women and children aged 12 years and older, generating evidence for populations that are often excluded from clinical trials. ‘Important step’ WHO emergencies director Chikwe Ihekweazu said the trial was set up to generate the rigorous evidence needed to determine whether the participating vaccines could protect people at risk. “If successful, this would be the first time we have clear evidence of vaccine efficacy against Bundibugyo virus — a major advance that could transform how we respond to this outbreak and prepare for future outbreaks and help save lives,” he said. Ebola, which spreads through contact with bodily fluids and causes a haemorrhagic fever, has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past 50 years. “Bringing this trial into the Ebola response is an important step towards addressing the urgent needs of affected communities,” said Steve Ahuka-Mundeke, the DRC Ebola response incident manager. The DRC declared its 17th outbreak of Ebola on May 15, and the WHO two days later triggered a public health emergency of international concern, its second-highest alert level. items.title: Remembering Alex Ekwueme amid growing anxiety, security concerns
items.description: By Chief Handel Okoli As Nigeria inches towards another general election, against a backdrop of political tension, growing anxiety, and genuine national security concerns, certain aspects of the life and times of one of our finest statesmen have assumed renewed significance. The ideas, convictions, and political philosophy of Dr. Alex Ifeanyichukwu Ekwueme, GCON, former Vice-President of Nigeria, deserve serious reflection as we consider the kind of country we wish to build. Dr. Ekwueme was born on 21 October 1932. Had he not passed away on 19 November 2017, he would have celebrated his 94th birthday on Wednesday, 21 October 2026. His death elicited an avalanche of tributes and encomiums from across Nigeria, reflecting the profound respect he commanded among people of different ethnic, religious, and political backgrounds. Even before his death, the late Professor Ben Nwabueze, SAN, had drawn national attention to Ekwueme’s enduring contributions in his 2013 book, The Legacies of Dr. Alex Ekwueme to Government and to Political and Social Development of Nigeria. Among the legacies highlighted were his formidable intellectual credentials as an asset in governance; his commitment to a strong multiparty system, constitutionalism, and the rule of law; his advocacy for the restructuring of the Nigerian federation; his proposal for the equitable distribution of political offices among the six geopolitical zones; and his remarkable public-spiritedness and philanthropy, which I once described as Ekwueme’s extravagant philanthropy. Yet, perhaps the most compelling of his legacies, and certainly one of the most relevant to Nigeria’s present political circumstances, was his altruistic and pragmatic approach to national integration. This is one of the fundamental challenges the Buhari administration failed woefully to address. Rather than build upon the emerging spirit of national reconciliation and integration, the administration, in my view, took the country in the opposite direction. President Jonathan had handed over the report of the National Conference to President Buhari, but the latter apparently had other priorities. An important opportunity to confront Nigeria’s unresolved national questions and build a more inclusive federation was consequently lost. Ekwueme understood that the survival of Nigeria as a united nation depended, to a considerable extent, on addressing the fears of domination, exclusion, and marginalisation among its constituent ethnic and regional groups. THE QUEST FOR NATIONAL INTEGRATION Following the end of the Nigerian Civil War in 1970, the urgent questions of national reconstruction, reconciliation, and the restoration of confidence among the country’s diverse peoples occupied a central place in political discourse. These concerns became particularly prominent during the formation of political parties in 1978, as Nigeria prepared for a return to civilian rule. The political parties recognised, to varying degrees, the need to accommodate the country’s complex ethnic and regional composition. The National Party of Nigeria (NPN), which eventually won the presidential election, adopted a political arrangement that reflected the importance of balancing interests across the North and the South in the distribution of key political offices. It was within this political atmosphere that Dr. Alex Ekwueme emerged as the NPN’s vice-presidential candidate, alongside Alhaji Shehu Shagari as its presidential candidate. The significance of the Igbo presence in the vice-presidential calculations of the major political parties of the period deserves particular attention. With the exception of the Nigerian People’s Party (NPP), whose presidential candidate, Dr. Nnamdi Azikiwe, chose Professor Ishaya Audu as his running mate, the other major parties also featured Igbo politicians as their vice-presidential candidates. These choices were politically significant. At the very least, they reflected an awareness of the need to broaden the political coalitions upon which the Nigerian federation rested and to reassure the Igbo people that, despite the devastation of the Civil War, they remained an integral part of the Nigerian project. It would, however, be a mistake to regard these political arrangements as merely symbolic. They raised a fundamental question about the future of Nigeria: could the country achieve genuine reconciliation and lasting unity without creating a political environment in which every major ethnic and regional group had a fair opportunity to participate in national leadership? The prospect of an Igbo man ascending to the presidency subsequently became a subject of considerable political sensitivity. It has been suggested that apprehensions about Dr. Ekwueme’s possible emergence as President, particularly in the context of political succession under the Shagari administration, formed part of the considerations surrounding the military coup of December 1983. While such claims require careful examination against the available historical record, they underscore a larger and more enduring problem: the difficulty Nigeria has faced in separating the legitimate pursuit of political power from fears about the ethnic or regional identity of those who might exercise it. The lesson is unmistakable. National unity cannot be sustained by rhetoric alone. It requires deliberate political arrangements, mutual trust, and a willingness to accommodate the legitimate aspirations of all sections of the country. FROM MILITARY RULE TO THE QUEST FOR A NEW NIGERIA The military coup that terminated the Second Republic in December 1983 abruptly ended the democratic experiment in which Dr. Ekwueme had played such a prominent role. He was subsequently detained by the military authorities and subjected to imprisonment. Yet, in a remarkable demonstration of intellectual resilience, that period of confinement provided him with an opportunity to reflect more deeply on the Nigerian condition and to nurture his ideas about the kind of country Nigeria ought to become. Rather than seize the opportunity to address the structural problems that had contributed to political instability, mutual suspicion, and the struggle for power, successive military administrations introduced institutional changes that, in my view, further complicated Nigeria’s national question. The creation of additional states and local government areas, the delineation of electoral constituencies, and the conduct and interpretation of population censuses became contentious issues in the struggle over political representation and the distribution of national resources. The consequences were particularly troubling for what is today the South-East geopolitical zone, whose concerns about representation and its relative position within the federation have remained important elements of the national debate. The point is not that every administrative or political change undertaken under military rule was necessarily designed to disadvantage a particular region. Rather, it is that institutional arrangements introduced without sufficient regard for fairness, transparency, and the confidence of all constituent groups can deepen existing grievances and undermine national cohesion. The failure of the Babangida administration to complete a credible transition to democratic rule, culminating in the annulment of the 12 June 1993 presidential election, further aggravated the national crisis and deepened public distrust of the political process. It was against this background of political uncertainty, institutional distrust, and unresolved questions of national identity that Dr. Ekwueme, having endured detention and imprisonment, began to engage more actively with like-minded Nigerians on the need to reconstruct the Nigerian federation on a more equitable foundation. His concern was not simply who would occupy the presidency at any given time. It was how Nigeria could evolve a political system in which the struggle for power would no longer be perceived as an existential contest among ethnic and regional groups. THE 1994/95 CONSTITUTIONAL CONFERENCE: A DEFINING MOMENT Dr. Ekwueme played a leading role in articulating the structural and constitutional issues confronting Nigeria. In this endeavour, he worked alongside other prominent Igbo leaders, including the Ikemba Nnewi, Chief Emeka Odumegwu-Ojukwu. The challenge before the South-East was not merely to secure immediate political concessions. It was to participate meaningfully in the reorganisation of the Nigerian state and advance constitutional arrangements capable of protecting the interests of all regions over the long term. Dr. Ekwueme’s contribution to the 1994/95 Constitutional Conference reflected his characteristic preference for altruistic intellectual engagement over political theatrics. He served on the Committee on the Structure and Framework of the Constitution, where he made significant contributions to debates on the institutional foundations of the federation. His performance earned him recognition as one of the outstanding delegates. Among the honours he received was an award from The Punch newspaper as its Most Distinguished Delegate. His approach demonstrated an important lesson in public leadership: political influence is not determined solely by the prominence of the office one occupies. It can also derive from the quality of one’s ideas, the depth of one’s preparation, the clarity of one’s vision, and the ability to persuade others through reasoned argument. Ekwueme understood that the national question could not be resolved by political slogans or temporary compromises. It required a serious examination of the structures through which power was distributed, resources allocated, and the constituent peoples of Nigeria represented. RESTRUCTURING AND THE SIX GEOPOLITICAL ZONES Among Dr. Ekwueme’s most consequential contributions to Nigeria’s constitutional discourse was his advocacy for restructuring the federation and organising the country around six geopolitical zones. The proposal was rooted in a practical understanding of Nigeria’s political realities. A federation as diverse as Nigeria could not achieve lasting stability if access to its highest political offices and the benefits of national development were persistently perceived as the exclusive preserve of particular regions or groups. It is important to appreciate the deeper logic of Ekwueme’s proposal. He was not simply advocating a convenient formula for distributing political offices. His vision was to reduce the desperation associated with political power by assuring every part of the country that it had a legitimate place in the national leadership structure. Where groups believe that political exclusion will permanently deny them access to influence, resources, and opportunities, competition for power can become bitter and destabilising. Conversely, where credible constitutional arrangements provide assurances of inclusion, political competition is more likely to take place within an atmosphere of mutual confidence. The six geopolitical zones were therefore more than geographical classifications. In Ekwueme’s conception, they offered a framework for promoting national integration, political accommodation, and unity. The proposal was understandably controversial. Any arrangement that seeks to alter an established distribution of political power will encounter resistance from those who benefit from the existing order. Yet resistance to such proposals does not diminish the importance of the questions they raise. Indeed, the continuing debate over restructuring demonstrates that the fundamental issues Ekwueme sought to address remain unresolved. His vision challenged Nigerians to look beyond the immediate question of who should occupy the presidency and confront the more consequential issue of how the Nigerian state could be organised to inspire confidence among its constituent peoples. ROTATION OF THE PRESIDENCY AND THE UNFINISHED PROJECT The constitutional deliberations of the Abacha era gave considerable attention to questions of political inclusion, the distribution of power, and the restructuring of the federation. Dr. Ekwueme was among the prominent advocates of arrangements designed to make the Nigerian political system more equitable and inclusive. The broader principle behind his six-zonal approach was straightforward: if the presidency rotated among the six geopolitical zones in an agreed sequence, every zone would have a reasonable expectation of producing a President within a defined period. Such an arrangement could also have a practical political benefit. By giving every zone a credible expectation of access to the presidency, it could reduce the incentive for political actors to treat every election as a final opportunity to secure power for their own region. However, an important distinction must be drawn between a constitutional proposal, a political understanding, and an enforceable constitutional provision. The six geopolitical zones have not been constitutionally entrenched as the exclusive units for rotating the presidency. This omission is significant. Nigerian politicians have often demonstrated a willingness to embrace the principle of zoning when it serves their immediate interests, only to abandon or reinterpret it when its consistent application would require sacrifice or accommodation in the broader national interest. The result is a political culture in which the language of fairness is frequently invoked, but the discipline required to sustain equitable arrangements is often lacking. Otherwise, why should a country that has repeatedly acknowledged the importance of geographical balance in political leadership continue to treat the six-zone principle as a matter of political convenience rather than a serious framework for national integration? Nevertheless, the principle underlying Ekwueme’s argument remains compelling. Had Nigeria adopted and consistently implemented an effective constitutional arrangement for equitable regional participation in the presidency, it might have reduced some of the recurring grievances associated with political exclusion and the distribution of national power. It would, of course, be an overstatement to suggest that rotational presidency alone would have eliminated every complaint about marginalisation, infrastructure, or the distribution of public resources. These challenges are influenced by many factors, including fiscal federalism, the distribution of federal institutions, the allocation of public investment, the quality of governance, and the independence of constitutional institutions. Yet a credible power-sharing arrangement could have made an important contribution to national confidence by demonstrating that Nigeria’s political system was designed to accommodate all its constituent parts. This, in my view, is the enduring significance of Dr. Ekwueme’s vision: to transform national integration from a political slogan into a practical constitutional commitment. AN UNFINISHED LEGACY As Nigeria approaches another general election, it is worth asking whether the country has sufficiently embraced the lessons of Dr. Alex Ekwueme’s political philosophy. Have we built a federation in which every region feels a genuine sense of belonging? Have we developed institutions that command the confidence of citizens, irrespective of ethnicity, religion, or political affiliation? Have we created a political culture in which the distribution of power is governed by fairness and mutual accommodation rather than by the fear of domination? These questions are particularly important for the South-East, whose concerns about political representation and equitable participation in national leadership remain central to the wider debate about restructuring and national integration. Nevertheless, the significance of Ekwueme’s vision extends far beyond the South-East. It is a vision for Nigeria as a whole: a country in which no ethnic group needs to fear another, no region should feel permanently excluded, and no citizen should be made to feel that national leadership belongs exclusively to a privileged section of the federation. True egalitarianism does not mean that every region must be identical in population, resources, or political influence. It means that differences should not become instruments of permanent exclusion or domination. It requires a constitutional order that recognises diversity while guaranteeing fairness, dignity, and equal citizenship. It also requires political leaders who understand that the long-term stability of the federation is more important than the immediate advantages that may accrue to one region, one political party, or one group of individuals. Ekwueme’s legacy challenges contemporary Nigerian leaders to look beyond the immediate calculations of electoral advantage and ask a more fundamental question: what kind of political system will leave the country more united, more stable, and more confident in its collective future? NORTH–SOUTH ZONING OF THE PRESIDENCY: A DISTORTION OF THE SIX-ZONAL VISION Let me state clearly, for the avoidance of doubt, that the current practice of zoning or rotating the presidency between the North and the South does not adequately reflect the essence and significance of Dr. Ekwueme’s six-geopolitical-zone approach. A North–South arrangement, in my view, falls short of the more inclusive vision underpinning the six-zonal framework. By reducing Nigeria’s complex geopolitical structure to two broad blocs, it risks overlooking the distinct identities, interests, and aspirations of the six geopolitical zones. The North and the South are not homogeneous political entities. Each comprises distinct geopolitical zones with their own histories, interests, concerns, and expectations. A system that recognises only two broad blocs may provide a measure of regional balance, but it does not necessarily guarantee equitable participation by all six zones. Most unfortunately, those who appear to have acquiesced in this arrangement include some of the very people for whose protection and political inclusion Dr. Ekwueme’s prescriptions were designed. His vision was not intended to replace one form of exclusion with another. It was intended to create a fairer political order in which every geopolitical zone would have a credible opportunity to participate in national leadership. The North–South formula, therefore, cannot be regarded as an adequate substitute for a genuine six-zonal framework. It may address the immediate question of balancing power between two broad regions, but it leaves unresolved the more fundamental question of equity among the six geopolitical zones. If Nigeria is genuinely committed to national integration, political equity, and a more inclusive federation, it must give serious consideration to the broader and more purposeful framework represented by six-zone rotation. This does not mean that zoning alone will solve Nigeria’s national question. Nor does it mean that the presidency should become a substitute for the wider constitutional reforms that the country requires. Rather, it means that equitable access to national leadership should form part of a comprehensive effort to build a federation in which every constituent part has a genuine sense of belonging. The objective should not be to confer permanent political advantages on any region. It should be to establish a credible framework of fairness, mutual accommodation, and shared national responsibility. That, in my understanding, is the enduring message of Ekwueme’s egalitarian philosophy. CONCLUSION: BEYOND TRIBUTES TO IMPLEMENTATION As we remember Dr. Alex Ifeanyichukwu Ekwueme, Ide Oko, on what would have been his 94th birthday, we should do more than celebrate his achievements. We should revisit his ideas, examine their continuing relevance, and summon the political courage to implement those that can help build a truly united and egalitarian country. Ekwueme’s life reminds us that patriotism is not merely about occupying public office, winning elections, or enjoying the privileges of political power. It is also about the willingness to challenge an unjust status quo, advance ideas that may not yield immediate personal benefits, and work towards a political order that gives every citizen and every region a fair opportunity to thrive. His legacy calls for a Nigeria in which national integration is not merely proclaimed but practised; in which constitutional arrangements inspire confidence rather than suspicion; and in which the pursuit of political power is moderated by a genuine commitment to fairness and the common good. The greatest tribute we can pay this distinguished statesman is not the eloquence of our birthday tributes but the seriousness with which we engage his ideas and the determination with which we pursue the national transformation he envisioned. May his enduring legacy continue to inspire the quest for a more united, equitable, and egalitarian Nigeria. Chief Handel Okoli is Former Special Assistant to Former President Dr. Alex Ekwueme; Former Special Assistant to Former President Olusegun Obasanjo on Special Duties. items.title: Woman, 65, becomes second patient to die of Ebola in Kenya
items.description: Kenya has recorded its second death from Ebola as it handles its first ever outbreak of the disease. A woman, aged 65, who was a close family member of the first victim, a man who had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo, died after being placed in quarantine, the health ministry said. Seven other Ebola patients were receiving treatment at two isolation facilities, it added. All the cases were within “one cluster, with no evidence of community spread”, the ministry said. More than 4,000 people have died in Africa since Ebola was confirmed in DR Congo in May, making it the second most deadly outbreak of the disease. Kenya’s latest victim was a “direct contact and close family member of the first case (deceased) and was under quarantine when she developed symptoms” on 13 October, the health ministry said. The first death, on 5 October, was that of a man who fell ill in September and was treated in several hospitals in DR Congo before arriving in the Kenyan capital, Nairobi, where he died a few days later. Those still being treated are three other relatives of the first victim, three health workers and a hospital cleaner. The US has warned its citizens against travelling to Kenya, while neighbouring countries such as Uganda, Ethiopia and Somalia are also on alert. Ebola is a rare but deadly disease caused by a virus. As the disease progresses, vomiting and diarrhoea develop and it can lead to organ failure. Some, but not all, patients develop internal and external bleeding. The disease spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids such as blood or vomit. The Bundibugyo species of Ebola is relatively rare, with no approved vaccine or treatment – though trials are under way. With more than 9,500 cases in DR Congo, Kenya faces a steady risk of new cases arriving across borders, according to the International Rescue Committee, which has been working alongside both governments to contain the spread. Kenya has introduced enhanced screening for travellers arriving from DR Congo and nine other countries it considers to be at high risk: Uganda, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, Angola, Zambia, Ethiopia, South Sudan and the Central African Republic. Travellers arriving from those countries are required to complete a digital surveillance form before boarding their flights, and to present a QR code to port health officials on arrival. Kenya also ordered enhanced public health screening of aircraft arriving from those countries, as authorities seek to prevent further imported cases. Within the country, the government has been sharing public messages to create awareness about Ebola, including encouraging people to promptly report any suspected cases and seek care at a hospital. It has also focused on hygiene and safety measures, such as washing hands and avoiding close contact with sick people.In another development, Nigeria’s health minister has said the country’s single confirmed case of Ebola appears to be genetically related to a strain identified earlier in Kenya. Professor Ali Pate said there was no evidence so far that the Kenyan patient had travelled to Nigeria, but that further testing was under way. He emphasised that Nigeria had so far recorded only one confirmed case of the virus. “We are conducting additional tests. Some of the results are negative, while others are pending,” Pate said. Health officials have been investigating whether Nigeria’s first case crossed paths with Kenya’s first patient. Both are believed to have travelled through Uganda’s Entebbe International Airport earlier this month.

items.title: Who recruits ad hoc workers for INEC?
items.description: When Nigerians discuss election preparedness, attention often turns to the chairman of the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, its national commissioners and the technology the commission plans to deploy. Read Also: 2027: Violence threatening polls But former INEC National Commissioner Mike Igini says the decisive test may lie further down the chain – with the temporary workers who manage voting and counting at polling units. “The people that are going to conduct these elections are not the regular permanent staff of INEC,” Igini said during a television interview. “Nigeria needs to focus on the people that are going to conduct this election.” These workers, including presiding officers, handle key tasks on election day. They verify voters, manage election materials and record results. If their identities or impartiality are in doubt, Igini argued, public confidence in the process could suffer before the results are even announced. He urged agencies that supply temporary election workers to ensure their lists are accurate and that those recruited are properly verified. He also called on INEC to check the lists it receives rather than rely solely on the agencies that submit them. The issue, he said, is that political interests could find ways to influence recruitment lists. He recalled an incident in Akwa Ibom State during his time as a commissioner, when he said officials found people on a list who were not staff of the university expected to provide workers for the exercise. “We discovered that mercenaries were sent in on that list,” Igini said. He added that a market woman told officials her name had been included and that she had come to attend training. Igini said the discovery prompted him to stop the training while the list was examined. The episode, in his account, showed how a process intended to draw qualified workers from established institutions could be vulnerable to interference. His concerns also extend to the recruitment of members of the National Youth Service Corps, NYSC, whom he identified as a key source of polling-unit officials. He called on the corps to protect the integrity of the names it submits to INEC and on the commission to verify the people assigned to election duties. “The list is infiltrated,” he said, describing what he believes can happen when recruitment is not sufficiently checked. He warned that a compromised list could put people at polling units who have not been properly vetted or trained. Igini cited a separate controversy from the 2023 elections in Rivers State, alleging that an ad-hoc worker who announced results in one local government area had claimed to be a lecturer at a college. He said journalists who checked with the institution could not find the person on its payroll. The claim, as presented in the interview, was not independently verified. Igini used it to argue that election authorities should be able to explain who is recruited, where the workers come from and how their identities and qualifications are confirmed. He said the problem was not simply whether a temporary worker had completed training. The commission, he argued, must also be confident that the person attending the training is the same person who will serve at the polling unit. That concern places responsibility on several institutions. Agencies that provide personnel must keep reliable records and protect their recruitment processes. INEC must scrutinise the names it receives, verify identities and supervise workers on election day. Political parties and their agents, meanwhile, have a role in observing the process and raising concerns through proper channels. Igini said INEC’s senior officials would not be present at every polling unit on election day. The work would be carried out by temporary staff under the commission’s supervision, making the quality of that supervision central to the process. He also noted that party agents and voters could help monitor what happens at polling units. He encouraged agents to audit election materials and document the process, including by taking a clear image or video of the original Form EC8A after results are recorded. “The power of the people at the polling unit is awesome,” he said, adding that voters would normally outnumber election officials there. His argument is that accountability should not end with the recruitment of workers. The public needs confidence that the people managing the vote are the people selected for the job, that they have been properly trained and that their actions can be checked. For the 2027 elections, that requires clear answers to basic questions: Which institutions will provide the ad-hoc staff? What checks will be used to verify their names and identities? How will INEC prevent political interference in recruitment? And what happens when an irregularity is discovered? Igini’s warning is that the credibility of an election can be weakened by decisions made long before ballots are cast. If the people entrusted with the polling-unit process are not properly recruited and supervised, he said, the result may be an election in which citizens struggle to trust the process. He advised: “The most important staff that Nigeria should focus on will be the presiding officers.” Vanguard News The post Who recruits ad hoc workers for INEC? appeared first on Vanguard News .
