items.title: Kadiatou Bangoura, boursière non-voyante, raconte son calvaire à Chypre du Nord : « J’étais seule dans la maison, enfermée, je ne sortais pas »
items.description: Bénéficiaire de la Handibourse, un programme financé par Winning Consortium Simandou et destiné aux étudiants en situation de handicap, Kadiatou Bangoura affirme avoir été contrainte d’interrompre son master à Chypre du Nord faute d’assistance adaptée à sa déficience visuelle. Revenue en Guinée depuis plus d’un an, elle réclame le rétablissement de ses droits et interpelle les autorités. De son côté, Ibrahima Sory Barry, chargé du suivi du projet au Service national des bourses extérieures (SNABE), apporte des précisions sur les conditions de prise en charge, les démarches entreprises et les raisons pour lesquelles la situation de l’étudiante reste, selon lui, complexe. « Moi, c’est Bangoura Kadiatou. Je suis une non-voyante, diplômée en histoire des relations internationales de l’Université Général Lansana Conté de Sonfonia. J’ai fait appel à la presse parce que j’estime avoir été victime d’une injustice de la part du SNABE, le Service national des bourses extérieures », explique-t-elle d’entrée. En 2023, Kadiatou Bangoura obtient une Handibourse, un programme destiné aux personnes en situation de handicap et financé par la société minière Winning Consortium Simandou. Elle fait partie de la première promotion composée de trois étudiants guinéens, envoyés à Chypre du Nord pour poursuivre leurs études supérieures. Mais pour la jeune femme, le rêve d’obtenir un master à l’étranger s’est progressivement transformé en une épreuve, marquée, selon son témoignage, par des difficultés d’adaptation et surtout l’absence d’un accompagnement approprié à son handicap. « Nous étions là-bas à trois, tous en situation de handicap, mais nous n’avions pas d’assistance » Kadiatou Bangoura affirme que le départ à l’étranger a été précédé de plusieurs difficultés. Initialement, les bénéficiaires devaient être orientés vers la Roumanie. Faute d’admissions, une autre destination aurait été envisagée. « Ils nous ont dit, dans un premier temps, qu’ils voulaient nous envoyer en Roumanie, mais qu’ils n’avaient pas obtenu les admissions nécessaires. Quand j’ai échangé avec le directeur, il m’a dit que leur plan B était la Turquie. À ma grande surprise, un jour, quand je suis allée au service, on nous a annoncé que nous étions inscrits à Chypre du Nord », raconte-t-elle. Avant leur départ, la jeune femme dit avoir attiré l’attention des responsables sur la nécessité de vérifier les conditions d’accueil des personnes handicapées dans le pays de destination. « Je leur proposais toujours de faire des recherches sur les conditions de vie des personnes en situation de handicap dans le pays où nous devions aller, pour éviter que le projet échoue. » Une fois sur place, elle affirme avoir découvert un environnement peu adapté à ses besoins. « Nous étions là-bas à trois, toutes des personnes en situation de handicap : deux personnes handicapées motrices et moi, qui suis non-voyante. Quand nous sommes arrivés, nous n’avions pas d’assistance. Nous avons même effectué seuls nos démarches administratives dans un pays que nous ne connaissions pas », déplore-t-elle. Selon son récit, les responsables de l’université d’accueil lui auraient fait savoir qu’ils n’avaient jamais encadré d’étudiante non-voyante et ne disposaient pas des dispositifs nécessaires pour lui permettre de suivre normalement les cours. « Ils ont fait des propositions au SNABE. Ils ont expliqué que, s’ils voulaient que j’étudie là-bas, il fallait mettre des mesures en place : acheter des livres en braille, des imprimantes braille et trouver quelqu’un qui puisse m’assister en classe, notamment pour prendre les notes pendant la première année, où nous devions apprendre l’anglais. » Faute de solution satisfaisante, Kadiatou Bangoura dit avoir demandé une réorientation vers une autre destination. « J’étais seule dans la maison, enfermée, je ne sortais pas » La jeune femme affirme que les démarches pour trouver une solution ont duré plusieurs mois, sans aboutir à une prise en charge adaptée. « Ils m’ont dit qu’ils allaient entrer en contact avec les partenaires pour voir s’ils acceptaient de chercher une autre destination pour moi. Un jour, ils sont venus me dire que les partenaires avaient accepté, mais à condition que je rentre d’abord au pays. J’ai dit d’accord, il n’y a pas de problème », relate-t-elle. Mais, selon elle, le retour en Guinée a également tardé. « Nous sommes restés dans cette situation pendant des mois et des mois. Quand je leur demandais d’acheter mon billet pour rentrer, ils ne le faisaient pas. J’étais seule dans la maison, enfermée. Je ne sortais pas parce que je n’avais même pas d’assistance. Étant non-voyante dans un pays que je ne connais pas, où je ne maîtrise pas l’environnement, je ne pouvais pas me déplacer seule. » Kadiatou Bangoura affirme avoir multiplié les démarches auprès du SNABE pour obtenir son billet de retour. « À chaque fois, on me disait que la demande avait été déposée auprès du ministre Diba Diakité, sous la tutelle duquel se trouve le SNABE, mais que le ministre n’avait pas encore signé. Je ne sais pas si c’était vrai ou non. Je ne suis pas là pour dénigrer qui que ce soit. Je suis simplement là pour demander justice et qu’on me rétablisse dans mes droits », précise-t-elle. Finalement rentrée en Guinée, elle dit n’avoir toujours pas retrouvé le chemin des études. « Depuis que je suis revenue, cela fait un an et quelques mois. Je n’ai rien. Quand je demande à reprendre mes études, on me dit qu’il n’y a pas de bourse. On m’a même dit qu’un boursier qui demande à rentrer et qui rentre ne fera plus partie des boursiers. Je ne sais pas si c’est un règlement, mais je trouve que ce n’est pas juste. » Pour elle, le problème ne se limite pas à l’interruption de ses études. Il concerne également la manière dont les besoins spécifiques d’une étudiante non-voyante auraient été pris en compte dans la mise en œuvre du programme. « Je me sens trahie par les autorités du SNABE. Je me demande si mon handicap n’a pas été utilisé pour protéger certains postes. Je suis partie avec le courage d’étudier malgré mon handicap. J’ai pris des risques, j’ai essayé de me battre, mais je n’ai même pas pu étudier correctement. Ce n’est pas normal que je vive cela », dénonce-t-elle. Son appel s’adresse directement au président de la République et au ministre de tutelle. « Je demande au chef de l’État et au ministre Diba Diakité de m’aider à être rétablie dans mes droits. On ne peut pas m’envoyer dans un pays où il n’y a pas d’assistance adaptée, me laisser revenir et ensuite me dire que je n’ai plus de bourse. Je veux simplement continuer mon master en histoire des relations internationales. » Au-delà de son cas personnel, Kadiatou Bangoura plaide pour une meilleure prise en compte des personnes handicapées dans les programmes de formation à l’étranger. « Je veux simplement un pays où les personnes handicapées bénéficient réellement d’une assistance. Je suis non-voyante, mais j’ai pris le courage d’étudier. S’il vous plaît, monsieur le Président, aidez-moi à ce que justice soit faite. » Ibrahima Sory Barry : « Le SNABE n’est qu’un pont entre la société qui finance et les étudiants » Interrogé sur cette situation, Ibrahima Sory Barry, chargé du suivi du projet Handibourse au SNABE, défend la gestion du programme et apporte des précisions sur les responsabilités des différentes parties. « Lorsque je suis arrivé au SNABE, j’ai trouvé ce projet déjà en place. Il était dans une phase stagnante. Ma première mission a été de le faire avancer avec l’aide du secrétaire hiérarchique que j’ai trouvé sur place », explique-t-il. Selon lui, la Handibourse est un programme conçu pour favoriser l’accès des personnes en situation de handicap à l’enseignement supérieur à l’étranger, grâce au financement de Winning Consortium Simandou. « Il faut préciser que le SNABE ne finance pas les études de ces étudiants. Nous ne donnons pas et nous ne retirons pas la bourse. Nous sommes un pont entre la société qui finance, Winning Consortium Simandou, et les étudiants, que nous gérons sur le plan administratif », soutient-il. Ibrahima Sory Barry indique que les engagements du partenaire financier sont définis dans une convention signée avec le SNABE. « Tout ce qui concerne le logement à l’étranger, le paiement de la scolarité et les équipements de travail didactique est pris en charge par Winning. C’est écrit dans la convention. En revanche, l’assistance personnelle n’y est pas prévue », précise-t-il. Concernant Kadiatou Bangoura, il affirme que des dispositions avaient été prises pour lui permettre de poursuivre ses études avec les outils qu’elle utilisait déjà en Guinée. « Avant leur départ, nous lui avons demandé comment elle étudiait à Sonfonia. Elle nous a expliqué qu’elle utilisait un ordinateur ordinaire avec une application de synthèse vocale qui l’aidait à suivre les cours et à prendre des notes. Nous avons transmis cette information à Winning, qui a procédé à l’achat d’un ordinateur pour elle, avec le dispositif de synthèse vocale qu’elle avait indiqué », explique-t-il. Pour le responsable, l’équipement informatique faisait partie des mesures d’accompagnement prévues, contrairement au recrutement d’une personne chargée d’assister personnellement l’étudiante en classe. « L’université n’a pas pu trouver un assistant correspondant à ses critères spécifiques » Ibrahima Sory Barry affirme que les difficultés de Kadiatou Bangoura sont apparues dès le début de son séjour, en raison de la nature de son handicap et des exigences liées à sa formation. « Les problèmes de Kadiatou ont commencé dès le début, parce qu’elle n’a pas le même handicap que les autres. Les deux autres pouvaient se rendre en classe et faire leurs activités sans assistance personnalisée. Pour elle, la situation était différente », reconnaît-il. Il affirme toutefois que le SNABE avait entrepris des démarches auprès de l’université pour rechercher une personne capable de l’accompagner. « Nous avons écrit à l’université pour demander si elle pouvait trouver une assistante. L’ancienne direction a même envisagé de voir si le coût n’était pas trop élevé, afin de financer cette assistance. Mais l’université n’a pas accepté la formule demandée », rapporte-t-il. Selon lui, l’établissement aurait expliqué qu’il ne pouvait pas trouver une personne répondant aux exigences formulées pour accompagner Kadiatou Bangoura pendant les cours. « La réponse officielle de l’université indique qu’après plusieurs tentatives et une analyse de la demande, elle n’a pas pu trouver un assistant personnel correspondant aux critères spécifiques de l’étudiante », affirme-t-il. Le responsable précise que les besoins exprimés dépassaient, selon lui, le simple accompagnement dans les déplacements. « Elle voulait une assistance personnelle en classe, quelqu’un qui puisse lui dicter les leçons et l’aider à suivre les cours en anglais. Or, l’université n’a pas pu répondre à cette demande. Elle nous a proposé d’explorer d’autres solutions, notamment les services de tutorat en ligne », explique-t-il. Pour autant, Ibrahima Sory Barry estime que cette difficulté ne signifie pas que le SNABE aurait abandonné le dossier. « Nous avons essayé de trouver des solutions dans la mesure de nos moyens et des engagements prévus dans la convention. Il faut comprendre que le projet était déjà engagé lorsque je suis arrivé. Je n’ai pas participé à sa conception initiale », insiste-t-il. Un retour en Guinée discuté lors d’une réunion en juillet 2025 Le chargé du suivi de la Handibourse évoque également une réunion tenue le 1er juillet 2025 avec les trois bénéficiaires et les responsables du SNABE, après l’installation d’une nouvelle direction générale. Selon lui, cette rencontre avait pour objectif de permettre aux étudiants d’exposer leurs difficultés et d’examiner les possibilités de résolution avec la nouvelle équipe. « C’était une réunion de prise de contact, mais aussi une occasion pour chaque étudiant d’expliquer les problèmes qu’il rencontrait. Nous avons examiné la situation de chacun et formulé des recommandations à l’endroit du partenaire », indique-t-il. Concernant Kadiatou Bangoura, il affirme que la possibilité d’un retour anticipé avait été évoquée en raison de l’absence de solution à ses difficultés. « Dans le rapport de la réunion, il est mentionné qu’elle avait sollicité son retour anticipé au pays. À travers le service logistique, consulaire et sécurité, le SNABE a procédé à l’achat de son billet de retour. Le départ était prévu pour le 5 juillet 2025 », déclare-t-il. Il ajoute que le SNABE avait recommandé de rechercher une autre destination où la langue d’enseignement serait plus accessible à l’étudiante ou, à défaut, de lui permettre de poursuivre sa formation en Guinée. « Nous avons recommandé, à défaut de la réorienter vers une autre destination avec une langue d’enseignement adaptée, de trouver une université en Guinée où elle pourrait continuer ses études. Qu’est-ce que nous pouvions faire de plus que cela, dans le cadre de nos responsabilités ? », s’interroge-t-il. Ibrahima Sory Barry affirme cependant que la suite des démarches aurait été compliquée par la position exprimée par l’étudiante après son retour. « Quelques jours après son arrivée, je l’ai appelée pour lui demander quand elle viendrait au service afin que nous puissions examiner les alternatives. Elle m’a répondu : “Je ne veux plus de votre bourse” », rapporte-t-il. Pour le responsable, cette déclaration a rendu la situation plus difficile à faire évoluer. « Peut-être qu’elle n’a pas obtenu ce qu’elle voulait. Mais nous étions toujours en contact avec elle. Nous cherchions une autre solution pour qu’elle puisse poursuivre ses études », soutient-il. La question des compléments de bourse L’autre point de désaccord concerne les paiements que Kadiatou Bangoura estime ne plus percevoir depuis son retour en Guinée. Sur ce sujet, Ibrahima Sory Barry distingue les dépenses prises en charge par Winning Consortium Simandou des compléments de bourse relevant du SNABE. « Les étudiants qui partent à l’étranger bénéficient de compléments de bourse versés par le SNABE. Dans le cas de Kadiatou, il s’agissait de 120 dollars par mois pendant dix mois, avec un montant spécifique pour les vacances. Mais lorsqu’un étudiant rentre au pays et ne poursuit plus ses études à l’étranger, les paiements sont suspendus », explique-t-il. Il invite néanmoins Kadiatou Bangoura à se rapprocher des services compétents pour vérifier sa situation financière. « Si elle estime qu’elle n’a pas reçu certains compléments de bourse, elle peut venir au service financier. Les décisions d’attribution, de renouvellement et de paiement sont disponibles. Elle peut vérifier ce qui lui a été versé et ce qui ne l’a pas été », affirme-t-il. Le responsable insiste sur le fait que le SNABE ne dispose pas, selon lui, d’une ligne budgétaire lui permettant de prendre en charge toutes les dépenses supplémentaires liées à l’assistance personnelle à l’étranger. « Une malvoyante dans une université normale, c’est vraiment difficile » Interrogé sur la question de savoir si les besoins spécifiques de Kadiatou Bangoura avaient suffisamment été pris en compte avant son départ, Ibrahima Sory Barry reconnaît la difficulté que représente son handicap dans un environnement universitaire non adapté. « Franchement, une malvoyante dans une université normale où nous avons étudié, c’est vraiment difficile pour elle d’étudier et de terminer ses études, parce que l’université n’est pas adaptée à son handicap. Si c’était une université spécialement conçue pour les personnes non-voyantes ou adaptée à ce genre de handicap, ce serait différent », admet-il. Il affirme toutefois ne pas avoir participé à la sélection initiale des bénéficiaires. « Personnellement, je suis venu trouver le projet. Je ne sais pas sur quelle base les étudiants ont été sélectionnés ni comment la destination a été choisie. Je ne suis pas là pour barrer la route à qui que ce soit. J’essaie simplement de faire avancer le projet et de trouver des solutions aux difficultés rencontrées », précise-t-il. Sur les accusations relatives à l’isolement de l’étudiante à Chypre du Nord, il affirme avoir été régulièrement en contact avec les trois bénéficiaires. Il indique également que, durant le premier mois, une autre étudiante aurait apporté une aide à Kadiatou Bangoura. « Je suis tout le temps en contact avec ces trois étudiants. Peut-être qu’elle ne m’a pas tout dit. Le premier mois, il y avait une étudiante qui l’assistait. Les deux autres bénéficiaires étaient également sur place », déclare-t-il. Ces éléments constituent sa version des faits, tandis que Kadiatou Bangoura affirme avoir vécu une période d’isolement faute d’un accompagnement adapté à ses besoins. Un master en suspens et une demande de rétablissement dans ses droits Au-delà des explications avancées par le SNABE, la situation de Kadiatou Bangoura reste marquée par une question centrale : celle de la poursuite de ses études après une expérience à l’étranger qu’elle juge infructueuse. La jeune femme ne demande pas seulement que les responsabilités soient établies. Elle souhaite surtout retrouver la possibilité de poursuivre son cursus universitaire. « Je suis partie pour faire mon master en histoire des relations internationales. Je suis revenue, je n’ai pas étudié et, depuis plus d’un an, je suis là sans solution. Pendant ce temps, les autres étudient. Est-ce que c’est juste ? Ce n’est pas juste », déplore-t-elle. Elle appelle ainsi le président de la République et le ministre de tutelle à intervenir pour qu’une solution soit trouvée. « Je demande qu’on me rétablisse dans mes droits. Je n’ai pas abandonné mes études. J’ai voulu apprendre malgré mon handicap. Je veux simplement pouvoir continuer mon master dans des conditions qui me permettent réellement d’étudier », insiste-t-elle. Entre les difficultés d’adaptation invoquées par l’étudiante, les limites de la convention de financement exposées par le SNABE et l’absence, à ce stade, d’une solution définitive, le dossier de la Handibourse pose la question de l’accompagnement effectif des étudiants en situation de handicap dans les programmes de mobilité internationale. Pour Kadiatou Bangoura, l’attente se poursuit. Son souhait reste le même : reprendre ses études et obtenir le diplôme pour lequel elle avait quitté la Guinée. Christine Finda Kamano L’article Kadiatou Bangoura, boursière non-voyante, raconte son calvaire à Chypre du Nord : « J’étais seule dans la maison, enfermée, je ne sortais pas » est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Phishing, comment reconnaître les messages frauduleux et s’en protéger ?
items.description: Des courriels aux SMS, en passant par les appels telephoniques, les tentatives de phishing se multiplient et peuvent pieger meme les personnes les plus vigilantes. Au Mali, plusieurs employes d'une entreprise ont recemment ete victimes d'un lien frauduleux utilisant le nom d'une institution financiere. Un expert en cybersecurite explique les methodes utilisees par les fraudeurs et les precautions a prendre pour eviter ces arnaques. Le phishing, egalement appele hameconnage, est une technique de fraude qui consiste a se faire passer pour une personne, une entreprise ou une institution de confiance. L'objectif est d'obtenir des informations confidentielles, comme des mots de passe ou des donnees bancaires, ou de pousser les victimes a envoyer de l'argent. Recemment, plusieurs employes d'une entreprise au Mali ont clique sur un lien frauduleux qui utilisait le nom d'une institution financiere. Alerte, le service informatique a reagi rapidement en procedant au changement de leurs mots de passe. Selon l'expert en cybersecurite Ichaka Diarra, les fraudeurs peuvent d'abord collecter des informations sur leurs cibles afin de rendre leurs messages plus credibles. Ils imitent ensuite les communications d'organismes connus pour gagner la confiance de leurs victimes. Modes operatoires Pour les inciter a cliquer, ils jouent souvent sur l'urgence, en evoquant par exemple un probleme de compte a regler rapidement. D'autres promettent des recompenses ou des gains pour attirer l'attention et pousser leurs interlocuteurs a agir sans prendre le temps de verifier. Les formes de phishing L'hameconnage ne se limite pas aux courriels. Les fraudeurs adaptent leurs methodes aux moyens de communication qu'ils utilisent pour atteindre leurs victimes. Le smishing designe les tentatives de phishing par SMS. La victime recoit un message contenant generalement un lien frauduleux ou une demande destinee a lui soutirer des informations personnelles. Le vishing repose, quant a lui, sur les appels telephoniques. Le fraudeur peut se presenter comme un agent de banque, un responsable administratif ou un representant d'une entreprise afin de convaincre son interlocuteur de reveler des informations confidentielles ou d'effectuer une operation risquee. Dans tous les cas, le principe reste le meme, instaurer un climat de confiance. Ainsi, tromper la vigilance de la victime et l'amener a agir dans l'interet du fraudeur. Les bons reflexes pour eviter les pieges Pour se proteger contre le phishing, Ichaka Diarra recommande de verifier l'identite de l'expediteur avant de cliquer sur un lien. En cas de doute, mieux vaut contacter directement l'organisme concerne en utilisant ses coordonnees officielles, plutot que celles fournies dans le message recu. Il est egalement essentiel de ne jamais communiquer ses mots de passe, ses codes confidentiels ou ses informations bancaires en reponse a une sollicitation suspecte. Une promesse de gain inattendue ou un message qui exige une reaction immediate doivent aussi eveiller les soupcons. Enfin, la sensibilisation aux risques numeriques reste indispensable, notamment dans les entreprises. Former les employes a reconnaître les messages frauduleux, a verifier les liens et a signaler rapidement les tentatives suspectes contribue a limiter les consequences de ces attaques. L’article Phishing, comment reconnaître les messages frauduleux et s’en protéger ? est apparu en premier sur Studio Tamani - Informations, débats, magazines : toute l’actualité du Mali, en 5 langues .

items.title: The DEI Language That’s Doing More Harm Than Good
items.description: Last week, Senator Edward Markey published a social-media post seeking interns for his Boston office. He wrote that “BIPOC, LGBTQ+, working class, veterans, and other underrepresented candidates with Massachusetts ties are encouraged to apply.” Outrage quickly followed: Critics treated the post not as a straightforward attempt to encourage diversity in job applications, but rather as a discriminatory signal that white men would be disadvantaged in hiring. The Manhattan Institute’s Christopher Rufo called the help-wanted ad an open violation of civil-rights law and urged a federal probe. The former Trump Justice Department appointee Theo Wold wrote that a goal of Democrats is to ensure that young white men “have no opportunities to find gainful employment.” One response to Markey stated, “If you are a young White man struggling financially, I understand your frustration with the Iran conflict and gas prices, but you must understand that this is the official hiring policy of the entire corporate world if democrats return to power.” Because X rewards inflammatory retorts more than intellectual rigor, these particular claims of racial grievance are easy for skeptics to dismiss as sensationalism. Urging certain groups to apply for a job is not proof of hiring discrimination against others. Some groups that Markey’s post mentioned, such as gay people, veterans, and the working class, include lots of white men. There is overwhelming evidence that the Democratic Party’s goal is not “no opportunities” for white men, and that corporations are not a left-identitarian monolith. Still, setting all falsehoods and exaggerations aside, Democratic elected officials have long been more likely than Republicans to favor policies that consider race and sex in employment decisions. These policies sometimes result in credible claims of discrimination against white and/or male candidates: Large nonprofits , major cities , multinational corporations, and prestigious law firms have all lost court cases involving employment discrimination against white people or men, or altered their employment practices under pressure from federal or state agencies that enforce civil-rights laws. Republicans generally treat such discrimination as a bigger problem than Democrats, even as most Americans—including a majority of Democrats and Democratic-leaning independents— reject preferential treatment in hiring and promotions for favored groups. Populist-right partisans are probably correct that they have a political opportunity in going after any left-leaning political, academic, or business elites who push such policies. [ Read: Democrats can’t let go of racial preferences. ] The issue may prove especially potent for men in Generation Z. As recently as 2019, just a third of young men perceived some discrimination against men in America. In 2025, 51 percent of young men perceived it. Those feeling aggrieved by Markey’s words should bear in mind that, at 80, his views about race were formed before the civil-rights era. For most of his life, identity politics in Congress favored straight white men. Perhaps he still perceives that all groups other than white men need reassurance, and would be surprised that young white men today have any such need. (His office did not respond to my request for comment.) But older legislators need to grasp that efforts to diversify organizations, many of which focus on new hires, mean that Gen Z has a unique experience of the job market. Exposing white men in this cohort to language that seems to treat them differently from other groups is particularly unwise––they are especially primed to infer discriminatory intent whether or not it is being implied. Cheryl Kaiser, a psychology professor at the University of Washington, researches how “well-intentioned organizational diversity initiatives create unintended consequences.” She told me in an email that, although outreach to particular identity groups is distinct from restricting hiring to those groups, “the mere presence of a diversity signal, not the signal’s actual impact in hiring decisions, can increase White Americans’ concerns that they’ll face racism.” (In fact, several federal and state laws prohibit discrimination based on race, sex, or other protected characteristics—and these are laws that are intended to protect everyone, not just women or people of color.) In scholarship published in 2021, Kaiser and her co-authors found that “simply exposing White Americans to organizational diversity signals” increased their perception of a bias in hiring against white men. That perception occurred “even with clear evidence of White advantage within the organization, a less-qualified White candidate, or abundant promotion opportunities for all employees. Nor was it limited to people predisposed toward biased beliefs: the effect did not depend on participants’ endorsement of group-based hierarchy or their level of racial ingroup identification.” In another research paper, from 2015 , Kaiser and her co-authors found that the mere presence of pro-diversity signals “cause White male mock job applicants to experience cardiovascular stress as well as anticipate experiencing discrimination when applying for jobs at these companies.” Of course, the fact that people perceive discrimination does not mean they are actually being discriminated against. And if diversity language were effective in contributing to more equitable hiring outcomes, even while upsetting a few overly sensitive sorts, there would be a strong case for retaining it. But Kaiser believes that “the types of diversity signals that cause backlash often do very little to effectively diversify the workplace.” Research she published in 2020 found that “racial minority employees sometimes see organizational diversity signals as overstating real commitment, which is linked to feeling less able to fit in or thrive.” Often, then, diversity signals confound all assumptions: “They don’t produce the hiring outcomes critics fear, they don’t produce the trust or inclusion benefits supporters are aiming for, and yet they still trigger the perceptual backlash described above,” Kaiser told me. To meaningfully reduce resentment, grievance, and reactionary identitarianism among young white men, Democrats should adopt rhetoric that unambiguously clarifies a commitment to equal opportunity. Some may find this advice frustrating. For decades, the political right insisted that racial preferences were immoral and illegal, and that diversity efforts should be restricted to outreach . Now they’re treating mere outreach as proof of illegal discrimination. But as Kaiser’s research shows, diversity rhetoric can have unforeseen effects. White identitarians would exist even in a world without bias of any sort in recruitment or hiring––but using language that fuels white identity politics, as Markey’s language did, is political malpractice that’s bad for Americans of all races, no matter how well intentioned it might be. Even if one argues that diversity advocates shouldn’t have to change how they communicate in order to avoid backlash, the reality seems to be that they do. As is often the case in politics, social progress requires forging broad coalitions of people who often disagree. That requires an understanding of psychology, attentiveness to possible sensitivities, and, yes, even compromise. Outreach that values diversity and inclusion is still possible. In 2015, the social psychologist Wiebren Jansen and co-authors found that “including the cultural majority group in an organization’s diversity approach” can help white men with a high need to belong feel included, and can increase support within organizations for diversity efforts. Senator Elizabeth Warren’s approach to recruiting interns is a good example of inclusive language. Her call for applications uses familiar and simple language, describing her office as “an equal-opportunity employer” that does not discriminate based on “race, color, religion, sex, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, national origin, age, genetic information, disability, or uniformed service.” Warren “encourages all individuals from all backgrounds to apply.” Whether you’re Black or white or trans or gay or working-class or a veteran, if you are wondering whether people like you belong, that approach leaves no ambiguity: You’re encouraged to apply. “All individuals” are.

items.title: The Armageddon Economy
items.description: Subscribe here: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube It can feel like an existential moment right now—one where many tech leaders are both warning against and accelerating the destructive forces of AI. But Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor argue that this could also be a turning point toward building something better. The authors of End Times Fascism talk with Galaxy Brain host Charlie Warzel about runaway wealth, the politics of AI, and how to prepare if the tech-bloated market crashes. The following is a transcript of the episode: Astra Taylor: You know, are there ways to deal with a crash that lets the people who’ve perpetrated this, like, eat the downside. Like, could this be an opportunity to get rid of some of the excess wealth and the inequality in this moment? Charlie Warzel: I’m Charlie Warzel, and this is Galaxy Brain . There’s all kinds of chaos in the world. There’s multiple wars. The ongoing climate crisis. It is a bizarre and existential moment. And Silicon Valley is not helping. AI researchers are quitting in droves, and they’re worried that what they’re building might kill us all. It’s easy, in this moment, to dismiss all of this talk reflexively—to see this as little more than a form of tech marketing. Or conversely, it’s easy to believe it all uncritically. But my guests today have a different framework from which to process this moment, both in Silicon Valley and in the rest of the world. In their new book, End Times Fascism , the writers Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor offer up an idea that what we’ve seen from tech leaders in the last decade—from the AI build-out to the tech leaders’ pivot to supporting and working with Donald Trump—is all part of a broader movement of politicians and titans of industry trying to consolidate power in a moment of global instability. That this movement is, in meaningful ways, circular. For example, the tech tools create the conditions for chaos, and then those same leaders capitalize on the chaos. Klein is a New York Times best-selling author and a professor of climate justice who has been interrogating corporate power for decades. Astra Taylor is a writer, documentary filmmaker, and an activist. Together their argument is an attempt to explain a theory of power here in this turbulent decade, and how it builds off of and is different from the previous eras. But I really wanted to bring them on to zero in specifically on the “end times” part of their argument. Because whatever you think about what’s going on with our tech leaders, it seems very clear that the industry has adopted a zealous, and even religious, attitude in recent years. Promises of both utopian salvation and apocalyptic destruction are now commonplace. Silicon Valley is currently enamored with and terrified by the prospect that they are building God. They’re asking the rest of us to have faith: to put our trust in the technology and in them. But what world are they really trying to build here? And how did we get here? Klein and Taylor join me now to talk about it all. Naomi Klein, Astra Taylor: Welcome to Galaxy Brain . Astra Taylor: Glad to be here. Naomi Klein: Thank you. Warzel: So I wanna just start straight off with definitions here. The book is called End Times Fascism . Let’s start with defining end-times fascism and also how it both iterates on and is different from previous forms of fascism. Taylor: We subscribe to a view of fascism as something that didn’t just emerge as a kind of rupture in Europe in the 20th century, but something as a through line. Fascism has precedence. So fascism is a form of far-right reactionary politics that uses democracy against itself, that creates kind of vertical alliances between corporate and political elites. It is an elite-led right-wing movement, and creates kind of solidarities with a group—classes of people we describe as the “injured powerful.” And so end-times fascism is our term for a form of fascism that is in dialogue, that is responsive to novel planetary-scale crises. So Hitler and Mussolini did not know a world with atomic weapons. That’s something that changes the nature of what it means to be human—the fact that we can cause that kind of annihilation. Wealth is extremely concentrated. It was concentrated then, but now is even more kind of globally connected and concentrated in the hands of single individuals, like someone like Elon Musk, the world’s first trillionaire. We also live in a world that is being destabilized by climate change. So, you know, the fascists of yore understood pollution in the sense of something localized, but they didn’t understand the way we’re altering the chemistry of the planet. That is a huge factor in our analysis, and of course now. All these threats are being compounded by artificial intelligence. And today’s fascists are responding to these very real risks by basically accelerating, by slamming their foot on the gas and basically deciding that they’ll protect their in-group, and believing that they’ll be safe no matter what. So that’s why we see, you know, all of these high-tech lavish bunkers and this drive to fortress the nation. So fascism is always a response to real crises. It’s always a response to threats from the left, threats of redistribution. But the nature of the threats that we’re facing have changed. And we have all changed, I think, in response to these crises. Warzel: Well Naomi, then maybe this is a moment to ask: Is there a distinction here between an opportunism—with taking some of these global crises, and, you know, you’re saying the reactionary nature is in response to that. Is it opportunism? Or is it trying to continue, in your minds, perpetuating that—because it is also very helpful to, you know, the causes of an oligarchical class? Klein: So fascism is always an alliance. This is something else that recurs through the history of fascism. The Latin word means “bundle”— fascia , right? So it always has these distinct elements. And the elements of the fascist bundle that we look at in the book—that we identify as being part of the far-right coalition that we’re writing about—include people who have a very literalist end-times religious belief, right? So they really do believe that we are entering the end of days. And we also look at people we’re calling “tech end-timers,” right? Who are very focused on AI, and they have a story that really echoes these religious stories about how a new age is going to begin, change absolutely everything. Maybe birth a new species. Summoning a god. Like, there’s a religious quality to the stories that some of the people at the forefront of AI are telling. And then we look at the mass ethno-nationalist base of the far right around the world. Not just in the United States, for whom the chosenness is citizenship, and the bunker is the nation-state. But only certain people get to stay. And they’re very focused on keeping people out, right? So in terms of whether it’s opportunistic or accelerationist, it depends on who we’re talking about. I think that for the religious members of this coalition, you know, some of it is just identifying the crises that Astra mentioned. Interpreting them as signs, right? As we face real ecological boundaries, lots of things that are accelerating pandemics are welcomed and interpreted as signs. But as this kind of millenarian fever takes hold, and there is this feeling among Messianic Jews and Christian Zionists that we really have entered the end of days. Then you get into a loop where—because you believe that the end times are upon us—you do accelerationist things, like you actively expect. Expand wars, right? So it isn’t just opportunistic; it isn’t just kind of like these things are happening anyway. It’s: Hey, let’s attack Iran; let’s expand the war to the whole region. All of this is good. The worse the better. Right? And this is the danger of this kind of religion—is that it interprets things that really are objectively bad as good, and has a built-in incentive to accelerate them. Not true of everybody who is Christian; not true of everybody who is Jewish. But it’s true of people who are the most kind of fundamentalist believers of this—these end-times prophecies. Then you have in the tech world, definitely you have opportunism. You know, we quote this now kind of famous correspondence between Peter Thiel and Jeffrey Epstein about: Okay, Brexit has happened; the U.K. economy is going down; it’s the era of collapse. You know, now it’s all about making money on the collapse, right? Return to tribalism. This is Epstein writing, right? And so I think that we are seeing a kind of Armageddon economy. You know, when I wrote The Shock Doctrine I wrote about disaster capitalism. This was more about taking advantage of punctuated shocks, right—like a war or a natural disaster. I think there is an economic shift going on now, where a lot of people are betting on bad times. Right? They are looking at the same forecast that we are, but they aren’t interested in thinking about how you mitigate them. They’re thinking: Okay, things are going down, but that doesn’t mean that we have to stop profiting. There’s money to be made in containing refugees. There’s money to be made in building prisons. And deportation flights. And mass surveillance. So it’s a pretty bleak economy. But it creates, once again, these negative incentives, right? Because once you’ve really invested in it, then you don’t want there to be good times, because good times are “bad.” And you know, we quote [Palantir CEO] Alexander Karp saying: “Bad times are good for Palantir, and that’s not good for the rest of us.” You know: We don’t want large parts of our economy that are very invested in these end times staying “bad .” Warzel: For this conversation, I wanna focus on that tech portion of your book. And I think you were speaking about the religious leaders, and the way that when you believe that you are in this end-times moment, this apocalyptic moment—you do accelerationist things. And I think, you know, when we’re talking about AI and the tech world as it is right now, a lot of people think—and you all write about AI as the creation of this, you know, godlike-superintelligence thing. Or whatever it is, right? Klein: Well, we quote them saying it. We don’t believe it. Warzel: Yes, you quote them saying that. But I also think, too, that the entire technology is in itself—it’s not just religious in what it could do, but it’s the entire technology is a faith-based technology. In the sense that you are always shadowboxing the future version of what this will be, right? The classic line is: This is the worst that technology will ever be. Just wait, just wait, just wait. And this idea that you are never selling anything that you currently have—you are selling the idea. And the way that sort of religious nature exists now, as the main form of marketing in the industry. As the main way that venture capital flows in. And that people, you know, gain a foothold in the industry and power. And so I think that is really interesting—the way that there is that parallel there. That the tech industry has sort of taken on a religious nature in just how it behaves. Taylor: Mm. Klein: Yes. Taylor: Yeah. I mean, and there was precedent for this. In the sense, I mean—if you go back to the old days, before they all came out as far right, I mean, we talked about the cult of the founder, right? I mean, they were described in the press as oracles, as prophets, right? They would be, like, pitching a delivery app, and people were like: You know, they’re bringing democracy. They’re bringing deliverance. And so that was part of their brand. And I think like any cult, when the evidence starts piling up against you, you dig in all the more. So I think your description of it as a “faith-based technology” feels really apt, right? It’s just like: Just believe; just put all the money in there. Just put all the resources in there. You know: Don’t doubt what we’re making. So, I don’t know. I mean, I think the lesson maybe here is as simple as “don’t worship capitalists,” right? Klein: But I think the imminence point is really key. Because, I mean—there’s always an imminence in capitalism. Where it’s just kind of always about to get better. The “trickle down” is going to happen. Like—just sort of pray to those gods, right? But there were still actual material products that were legible; that were kind of delivering the things that they said that they were going to deliver. And that people were paying money for. So I don’t think we have ever had as much of the global economy based on a bet of something that is supposedly about to happen—but that doesn’t line up at all with the product that is actually being sold. Right? So that sort of sense of living in the “about to,” living in the imminence: I don’t think we’ve ever been sort of not where we are, but in the about to be. And that does feel quite religious. Warzel: And there’s an odd dynamic to all of this, as well. As you mentioned the economics of the AI boom and everything being built toward this speculative future. But there’s also now—because of the amount of investment, because of how predicated the economy is on Nvidia and the Magnificent Seven stocks—there is also this apocalyptic quality to all of this. Where if the music stops, if the investment stops coming in, right, then you have this specter of an absolute bubble burst. A huge, 2008-style crash, taking everything with it. On the other side of it, there is this “We are fulfilling the promise of this investment.” And then there is all kinds of economic upheaval. And you know, rewriting the social contract, and all the things that these people are talking about. Which are in their own sense very apocalyptic, as they are so disruptive. And so it feels like no matter where you are, you’re boxed in at least narratively—with this idea that something massive is going to happen. Taylor: Yeah. Klein: Yeah. Well, and it’s not our imagination. I mean, we are being conscripted into this dream whether we like it or not. The way the SpaceX IPO was structured, right? Where just like—rather than having a wait period before the stock is in everybody’s pension who has a pension, right, they change the rules. So you have no choice but to be part of this massive gamble, right? That is all based on this extraordinary claim that in the future, this nonprofitable part of the company, the AI division, will eventually have a market worth $28 trillion. It’s just wild, right? Warzel: I’m curious: In your minds, what is the world that the tech right is trying to build? As in this whole group investing in all these different technologies. You know, from the things that Musk is doing to things that Palantir are doing. Like, what is the world that you see them trying to build right now? Klein: I think that there are different visions, and then there are hedges to those visions. And some of those hedges might be: Well, if this all goes down we’re gonna just go to our corporate city-state in Honduras. And if that doesn’t work, we’ll go to our bunker in New Zealand. Or if that doesn’t work, we’ll go to the one in Argentina. And maybe we’ll also build a space colony. Like there’s a lot of different stories being told. I don’t think there’s one coherent, like: “This is our Eden.” So they need bunkers to protect themselves if this all goes very wrong. I don’t think that the kind of bunkers are their utopia. I think the utopia, really, is one of dematerialization, if that resonates at all. Like, I think that this idea of kind of being free from the material world—and I think this is actually the most religious part of it—is that the whole story of modern capitalism has been about leaving as much of the physical world behind, and with its obligations, as you possibly can. So first, companies declare: Well, we’re not actually making products; we’re making brands. And other people can make the products. Right? But then it’s like—even that, you know: We’re not publishers; we’re just platforms. So we want the profits, but we don’t want the responsibilities. And AI is the ultimate version of this. Where you actually kind of can upload your consciousness. You can live forever; you are free of the physical world, and you’re just betting on a machine world. So if there is a utopia, I think it’s being free of workers, infrastructure. Like, they don’t want to own their own data centers. I think they want to float upwards. Warzel: In your guys’ estimation, has this always been the project? Because for some, it seems yes, right? You have the Peter Thiels—always been reactionary, even early on questioning democracy as a useful concept to him and other people. Musk has been obsessed with transhumanism. But there’s also a lot of people who, I would argue, have come into this kind of bumbling, right? Like, they just wanted to build social networks or apps. Or, you know, make a website to rank who’s hotter in their dorm, and kind of stumbling into these roles as these new titans of technology and industry. And there was this liberal bent in Silicon Valley for a while, or at least a seemingly liberal facade in Silicon Valley. Does that feel like opportunism to you all, in the recent rightward pivot that a lot of these tech founders have had? Or do you think that there is something inherent in the project that you said—of sort of leaving the material world behind, being fully in the cloud, as it were—that would make it so that it was always going to lead to where we are now? Taylor: So I think we would argue that different conditions bring out different responses, different potentialities in people, different facets of them. I mean, I don’t think we should underplay how strong a right-wing bent there was in Silicon Valley. I mean, scholars have written about cyber-libertarianism and the kind of, you know, right-wing politics. So yes, you know: socially liberal but economically conservative. Or sometimes, in the case of Peter Thiel and his friends, just overtly reactionary and antidemocratic. So those ideas have been there, but they were tempered by the political and economic conditions. So I mean, I think there was a period when they’re building social media; they’re promising to democratize our culture and, you know, make the world a better place, where they could justify their extreme wealth. In terms of meritocracy, right? It still kind of fits in that paradigm. Like: We’re the smartest guys in the room. We’re the founders, and you all should bow down to us. But, you know, they were still kind of saying there would be these socially beneficial effects. In around 2014, 2015, when a “tech lash” started growing on the left or the right, that was challenged, right? I mean, so we argue that fascism, again, is always a response to crisis and a response to threats of redistribution. A threat from the left. And the tech lash was really pivotal. I mean, workers started organizing at these companies and demanding unions, and Me Too happened. And that was a very active force in Silicon Valley. Workers were saying: We want stronger environmental protections. Cities were saying: We don’t want your AI city. We don’t want sidewalk labs. Right? Countries were saying: We want privacy protections. Like, modest privacy protections would be nice. Right? Klein: The European Union. Taylor: Right. And so it was an affront to these guys and to their sense of themselves, but also to their business model. And I think they knew, rationally, that rolling out AI would be even more difficult, right? That it would receive even more of a pushback. Because most people are not clamoring for technology that threatens to take all the jobs, fill the internet with slop, possibly cause, you know, delusions in their friends and family members and children. And so they knew this. And they were already losing popularity. So I think these guys in that sense, you know—it’s a time for using the power they had amassed, right? And you know, we detail in the book why we think that they went in so hard with Donald Trump. And ultimately, we think it’s because of the material choice before them. They wanted to roll out AI without regulations. You know, with whatever energy they could get their hands on. They understood that to Trump, he’d love that it was gonna burn a lot of fossil fuels and boost the economy. And so they made a conscious deal. Warzel: So this case, that this rightward pivot has so much to do with the material needs of the tech companies responding to the AI build-out. What they need—both the lack of regulation, but also having, you know, friendly people like David Sacks. Who is a Silicon Valley insider who becomes the AI and crypto czar in the Trump administration for a while. You argue that, and it’s— Klein: I think he still has a lot of power in this administration, though he doesn’t have that position anymore. Warzel: Yeah; I mean, he just had dinner with a bunch of the AI executives as they’re talking about trying to “pace the frontier.” He’s definitely still in that mix. But there’s also this side of, you know, the founder psychology; as you said, the tech lash being this big part of it. How much do you weigh that? Taylor: Mm-hmm. Klein: Tech lash intersecting with AI, right? And this doesn’t start with ChatGPT, as you know, right? Like I wrote a piece about [former Google CEO] Eric Schmidt and the way he was pushing AI during the pandemic. First of all: The pandemic was very profitable for these tech companies, right? Because we’re all at home on our screens. Those of us who were not, you know, frontline workers. Right. Warzel: The Zoom revolution, yeah. Taylor: The Zoom boom. Klein: And it was the Zoom boom, and they all like—didn’t they double their wealth in the first two years? The billionaires and the tech billionaires? And the data-center build-out was frenetic in that period, right? Because so much streaming was happening; so much gaming was happening. And Eric Schmidt went on this big push of like: Isn’t Zoom school great? Isn’t telehealth great? Isn’t it like, maybe we should be more like China? And he made all these presentations in Washington about how the biggest problem with the U.S. in winning the AI race with China was all of these pesky privacy protections. Like, protecting people’s health records. And the fact that people didn’t want their kids under surveillance, and the fact that they didn’t want smart cities. And the whole frame was like: China is able to do all of this, because they have no privacy protections. And boo-hoo, the U.S. does, and the European Union is placing even more. Right? And so we see this moment that we’re in and the alignment with Trump as a revolt of the elites against regulation, and a very strategic alignment with someone who was sociopathic enough to let them do it, right? Because Trump’s relationship to AI and any other existential risk is just like: We all die sooner or later, you know? Warzel: You know, if you simply list off what AI is as a technology, and its promises, there’s something that I think ends up being pretty striking. Right? You have a technology that is trained on the ill-gotten, mostly, output of most of humanity. Requiring these material economic investments that are essentially unprecedented, and would yield unprecedented wealth and disruption, as we’re saying. And then this arguably quite false idea of creating perfect automated efficiency in markets and workplaces—such that humans aren’t really needed at all, right? And in that sense, it feels very end-timesy to me. Not in the sense that it will bring about the apocalypse per se, but in that there’s really nothing left for capitalism to do if it succeeds. And so my question to you: Is AI the final boss of capitalism? Is there anything left after it? Taylor: I mean, that’s interesting. You know, other people have phrased this like: So are these guys saying that AI is actually gonna bring about communism? Right? Like that’s the end point, because it’s, you know, sustainable super-abundance or whatever. Like, in this future you’ll never have to work again, and it’ll be leisure for all. So I mean, you know: I think the answer is no. Because their vision is not gonna come true as they are describing it, right? I mean, one of the recurring motifs of our book is that a group’s apocalyptic fantasies don’t have to be literally true. Or rarely are; never literally true. But they can cause a lot of havoc and a lot of damage regardless. Warzel: Right. Taylor: So I think they’re going to cause a lot of harm as they chase this vision. But there’s all sorts of questions that their end goal raises, right? Which is like: Yeah, how does capitalism work if people don’t have jobs and don’t have money? Like, okay—so you’re talking about a no-consumer future? It obviously gets to the point where they haven’t really thought this out. They’re just in the race, and they’re fine if they’re racing us off a cliff. And, in fact, the market seems to be catching up, right—with all the recent headlines about the fact that so much of this AI debt is actually now distressed, and the whole house of cards appears to be wobbling. Klein: And this is where I think their various escape plans do bear some attention. Because I think that there is this way that this is just all a massive gamble—and they do know it. Like, whether they know that it’s all going down or just part of it. I’m not gonna guess there. But I do think that all the hedges—and all the ways in which they have Plan Bs and Cs, right—is like if this goes down. You know, if say SpaceX valuation just seems to be fictional, seems to be notional, right? Like, I mean, and laughable. And everybody is just agreeing to go in it. Warzel: It’s about extending the light of consciousness throughout the universe. That’s like in the prospectus. It’s truly an actual dream. Like it is a fan-fiction scenario. Taylor: Yeah. Klein: Right. But I guess we’re pretty focused on what happens when this does pop, right? Whether it all goes down or partly goes down. What if their whole business model has been built on theft—Astra has called it “theft tech,” which I actually think is a very good phrase to describe a lot of AI—what are we owed before they get paid back? And how do we structure—like, how do we make sure that they aren’t able to just leave us with all the distressed assets? Where a few ultra-rich people pull off what in the book we call the “wealth rapture.” Right? Where they just ascend to their gated cities of various kinds and are like: Sorry, suckers . Because I do think that’s one of the futures that we’re looking at. And I think that they’ve structured their companies in a lot of cases where their personal wealth will be okay. And they do have various escape plans, and the rest of us get stuck with all of the risk of this. And we just have to have our eyes open about it. Warzel: You mentioned a couple—that’s one of the scenarios you’re looking at if this goes sideways. What are some of the other ones that you’re thinking about? Taylor: I mean, I think that we saw this with the recent Axios reporting that the heads of these companies are doing these disaster-scenario plannings. Right? They’re like: What if there’s a massive cyberattack that uses our agents, and then the public gets really mad at us? So the “disaster” for them—I mean, this is also a tell. The disaster for them is less the potential catastrophe—the cyberattack, the critical infrastructure going down—than the public’s response. And the fact that it could be a PR disaster for them in a moment of democratic leverage. So I think, you know, we should hedge too, and we should prep too. Like, we don’t know exactly what the unraveling of this bubble in this sector will be, right? Even the term crash implies something going down—like the sort of 1929 stock-market vision. And it doesn’t actually necessarily have to unfold like that. So there could be, you know, financial collapse of some kind of the sector. Or there could be some sort of disaster. So you mentioned the 2007 bailout. I mean, the thing about that is—you know, the money in that crisis was much more systemic. In the sense that it was banks and people’s literal homes, right? I mean so much of the capital involved. There’s huge amounts of capital in the data-center boom right now, and in AI, but a lot of it’s from private hedge funds, and a lot of it is from private capital markets. Are there ways to deal with a crash that let the people who’ve perpetrated this, like, eat the downside? And I think we really should be on—could this be an opportunity to get rid of some of the excess wealth and the inequality in this moment? We also know from the COVID pandemic that it’s possible to pop up a welfare state almost overnight. Right? The government actually can do things pretty fast when there’s a crisis. And I’ve also been thinking a lot about the Silicon Valley Bank bailout. And how that was not a, you know, critical systemic bank. And so I think—and I’m not the only one to say this. Alexis Goldstein, who is at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, and others have written about how SVB should have—maybe they should have let it fail. And so I think we should look at the past, and look at how moments like this too often have actually led to increased inequality and pernicious consequences. And just be like: How do we, if there’s a crisis moment—how do we respond? And how can we ensure that ordinary people are helped, and that the executives who perpetrated this are held accountable? Warzel: It does strike me though too that obviously the rub in that is the way that, you know, retail investing—and obviously not everyone has money in the stock market. But how much that retail investing in people’s, you know, 401(k)s and pension plans and all that are tied up in these again, these “Magnificent Seven” tech stocks. Taylor: Yeah. I just want to say the organizer in me is like: We need a mass movement that restructures retirement in America. 401(k) is a pretty recent invention. Like, why is this the mechanism through which we guarantee—and don’t guarantee, frankly, undermine—security in old age? Klein: So the point is, Social Security came out of the market crash of 1929, right? I mean, why the unfairness of that produced fairness, right? And the thing about AI—and this has been coming up for us a lot on our book tour over the last month—is: The offer of it really is only seductive, only appealing, once we’ve already destroyed and cut our social and care infrastructures to the bone, right? Like—if your kids are being taught by a teacher who’s allowed to be as great a teacher as they want to be, with relatively good student-teacher ratios? And they’re able to, you know, use their creativity and love of learning? Then the idea that they could be easily replaced with a chat bot is absurd. You know that, right? But if you’ve already cut your public education system to the bone? If you’re crowding 35 kids into a classroom. If your teacher is completely overworked and overstressed and being told that they need to teach to the test anyway. Then it’s really all just about, you know, checking boxes and a multiple-choice exam. That is something that—if you then come in and be like “Everybody can have their AI tutors,” that’s a lot more appealing, right? Or if we’re already neglecting our elders, and they’re living alone and isolated, and we’ve destroyed the infrastructure where they used to be able to hang out and have fun? Then the idea that they could be made a little bit less lonely by talking to a chatbot then becomes appealing. Right? So this will be a moment when we can decide to invest in people, infrastructure. Which is one of the things that we hear from folks who are fighting data centers in places like Memphis. Like: Why are we getting these massive data centers instead of a community center or public transit, or any of the things that we need? Right? And so there is this interplay between our neglect of the animate human physical world and the offer of AI. And that is—I think we need to go that deep in the correction of thinking about “How do we respond to this crisis?” Taylor: Yeah. And I just want to say, though: Part of what’s maddening is, as you just said, the SpaceX perspective—which is like science fiction—is somehow taken as serious in our culture. But the idea that, “Hey, we could have a different kind of retirement system, where people are taken care of in old age” seems completely absurd. But we got Social Security after the crash of 1929, after the Great Depression. But also, we only got it because old people were organized. There’s something called the Townsend movement . And like, millions and millions of old people who were broke and had no real power were like: We deserve to have an income from the government. Like: We deserve to live . And they were incredibly persistent, and they put this demand on the table that was completely unprecedented, because Social Security didn’t exist. And now we live in the world they created. So we have to be ready. This is our version of prep, right? We have to be ready with the infrastructure. And with the demands that, yeah, seem crazy today, but might just be common sense when we make it through to the other side. Warzel: So let’s talk about one of the roadblocks to that. Which is obviously the politics of all this. A defining feature, as you all have written about, as I’ve written about, of our era. And this argument that you have is that we’re living in a time of genuine elite impunity. Klein: I’m so glad. I was excited to talk to you about impunity. That was such a great essay of yours. Warzel: Here we go. This week, as we’re recording this, The New York Times has reported that Musk, world’s richest man, personally invested $366 million so far in this election cycle. It seems that Musk’s wealth, especially here in politics, is just a genuine chaos agent, right? It is very hard to exact a financial toll on him, as things are right now. And he’s able to use his money—he’s purchasing not only influence but communications infrastructure. Buying Twitter, turning it into X and this political weapon. What does the world do about this man? Taylor: So I think the first thing to do is to settle into how not okay this is, and how deeply anti-democratic this is, and how offensive it is. And then yeah—we have to organize. I mean, you know, he has had some big losses, right? Remember the whole Wisconsin Supreme Court race, where he even went like dancing around with the cheese on his head? So I think people need to show up and vote. And then we need to build a serious mass movement that’s focused on money out of politics. And I think that this is another issue that has the potential to be really bipartisan, just like the data-center movement. You know, the polling is overwhelming on this issue, but there isn’t a lot of mobilizing around it. In part because a lot of the civic infrastructure in this country is donor funded. And so, donors are not making this a key priority. But I think citizens have to. And the time is right for something that, you know, gets at that core poison in our politics. Which is wealth and power. And then, I mean, ultimately the point is—you know, we argue in the book that this really isn’t about these individual men and their pathologies and their wounded egos or whatever. It is about the wealth itself. Klein: And a belief that their wealth should buy them impunity. That the point of having hundreds of billions of dollars, or maybe a trillion dollars, is that of course the rules don’t apply. Warzel: It does seem to me—and my kind of theory, around a lot of the data-center stuff, and the fact that you see a lot of protest from each side, and this very public distaste with not only data centers but a lot of artificial-intelligence technology being foisted on people. And then having Donald Trump kind of double down on this. To me, it feels like the beginnings of a politics that doesn’t actually focus on this one guy. It feels like an opportunity. It feels like a place that, you know, where this volatility could come in. And that’s what I think is really interesting about the fact that he doesn’t seem to really—as someone who, you know, usually can ride a lot of these waves—he doesn’t seem capable of doing that. But I want to actually use that to press here on feasible solutions. And people are so mad about the incursion of AI into real communities, and the use of natural resources. Or how loud they are, or the fact that the resources in their town are going toward a data center instead of toward other infrastructure that they need. And I talked to Democratic consultants who are like. This isn’t just the issue; it’s like the issue that should just be winnable. And yet, I don’t know if there is a truly coherent politics around it. So in your minds, what is it that politics around AI need to look like going forward? Into 2028? Taylor: Yeah. I mean, I think there’s different approaches and different debates within the Democratic Party. My position is always that, you know, it’s good when people are at a place like “the polling against data centers is encouraging.” People are not fans of AI. They don’t trust the tech oligarchs. But also, you know, we as political actors need to nurture that perspective and give it shape, and expand it into something that is a broader politics, right? Like, we’re not just engaging with something that’s frozen. And so I think, you know, it is pretty inchoate. But there are people who are like, This is just a NIMBY movement. Or it’s just about, you know: People just don’t like the local data center, but maybe they actually kind of use AI when they say they don’t like it. But I think my perspective is that it’s tapping into a bigger set of anxieties. Like: What kind of future is on offer? Who makes the decisions in our world, right? Because so many of these data centers come under the cover of NDA. It’s like: What is work? What is purpose? These are really meaningful, powerful things for us to tap into. And they’re about much more than tech. We have to understand it as embedded in a broader society in social conditions. And I think with AI, we need to do the same. Like this isn’t—we can’t separate AI from this question of “how do we structure our retirements?” Right? As Naomi said: Are our schools well funded? Do our jobs pay us enough to live? This is a moment when we really need to invest in the things human beings need to live well. Like—if we need to invest in our schools, invest in health care, invest in housing, invest in human beings doing the meaningful work. And I feel like that will resonate powerfully in this moment. And then if people can deliver on that, I think it could change our politics. Right? Warzel: I find that to be a really important point in all this. I’ve been writing a lot about this moment as a crisis of agency, right? One side is this crisis of agency that’s being manufactured by Silicon Valley. Which is saying: We’re going to enact our agency to take away yours and give you these tools that do everything for you. Taylor: Mm-hmm. Warzel: But on the other side, I think there is this huge conversation of: “What is a human for?” Which is exactly what you’re saying and alluding to. And thinking of the crisis of agency as an opportunity to reopen—because we are all having, whether we believe in it or not, we’re having lots of very weird existential conversations, right? About everything. Klein: Yeah. And, you know, some of them are good, where we are. Like, I’ve seen some really beautiful conversations happening, where visual artists and musicians are really talking about what it takes to make visual art, and what it is like to do that labor, and why it matters. And I don’t think that we’ve had many spaces to like just talk about why making art matters. And what it is actually like from the artist’s perspective to do it. Or even an interesting conversation that I heard, you know, with a mathematician about what it is like to solve a math problem. And I just—I’ve never actually heard a mathematician describe it so beautifully. So I think those conversations—where we’re kind of getting back to basics about what it is that we love about what we do, and what each other does. And can we find some wonder in that and marvel in that? So that we are less susceptible to Sam Altman telling us intelligence is something that is like a utility that can be supplied? And so is art, and it’s like a vending machine and it can just spew it out, right? So, I think we’ve been—like I was saying before, the more mechanized we become, the easier it is to just let AI fill in the last step, right? Like, the more we act like robots online, the more we’re replaceable by AI bots. So we’re gonna have to become more human. Like, figure out how to become more human and irreplaceable. But yeah—I think it’s quite a spiritual moment, in a way. And a lot of people are stepping into that. Warzel: I wanna end on a point here and get your thoughts—which is that one reading of End Times Fascism , paired with the interpretation of the rightward pivot in Silicon Valley, is that a lot of people, I think, were fooled or simply unable to pay attention to what was going on. And that the tech giants and their leaders built these tools that they argued would democratize voices. That would bring people together, would expand opportunity, get rid of gatekeepers. And what they’ve done instead is create something different. This redistribution of power and control and money—all in their favor. Maybe it’s, you know, a mirror world of the techno-optimism, right? And say that the end of Trump, down the line, marks the data-center backlash. All that marks a genuine resistance to this. And say we start to get some accountability for the end-timers. We start to get, you know, steps toward regulation. How do we stop this from happening again? How do we recognize this before it’s too late? Taylor: I think this is why it’s really important to have an understanding of, and criticism of, capitalism as a system, actually. Because that is part of what got us into this mess. So, you know, I’m thinking again about the sort of era you just described, where they were promising to bring democracy through social media. And there was, I remember a piece, by Lawrence Lessig. Who is quite an influential critic of all the ways our democracy is broken. But he’s essentially saying, you know: We need to cheer on the Googles and Facebooks of the world over the old-media dinosaurs. And it was like, because they’re new, right? Because they’re new. They’re the disruptors. They’re disrupting the dinosaurs. And it was like, yeah, but they’re what is going to make them different, right? Once they disrupt the old-media ecosystem— and they are the new platforms, the new gatekeepers—why should we trust them anymore? So I think understanding the way we are in an economic system that concentrates wealth—where people are relentlessly pushed toward endless growth, right? And endless resource consumption is really critical. At one point in the book, we describe fascism as capitalism’s threat response. This is a movement of corporate and political elites to defend their power and their wealth. And I think it will do us a lot of favors to think systemically like that. Because then we can think about: What’s the scale of the solutions? Right? Like, what do we actually need to ensure that we don’t just watch another terrifying sequel? Warzel: Naomi Klein, Astor Taylor. Thank you very much for coming on Galaxy Brain . Klein: Thank you so much. Warzel: That’s it for us here. Thank you again to my guests, Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor. If you liked what you saw here, new episodes of Galaxy Brain drop every Friday. items.title: Gao : indignation après une agression sexuelle présumée à l’hôpital régional
items.description: L'hopital regional de Gao reagit apres l'agression sexuelle presumee d'une patiente hospitalisee en reanimation, decedee quelques heures plus tard. Le bureau syndical presente ses excuses a la famille et a la population, tandis qu'une enquete a ete ouverte par la gendarmerie. Dans la ville, l'affaire suscite indignation et incomprehension. Le bureau syndical de l'hopital regional de Gao est sorti de son silence. Il reconnaît les faits rapportes, presente ses condoleances a la famille de la victime et lui adresse ses excuses, ainsi qu'a l'ensemble de la population. Selon Boubacar Issa Toure, porte-parole du syndicat de l'etablissement, le suspect presume serait un ancien stagiaire qui ne fait pas partie du personnel de l'hopital. Il serait actuellement en fuite. La gendarmerie a ouvert une enquete afin de faire la lumiere sur cette affaire. Le syndicat affirme etre en contact avec la famille de la victime. Face a l'emotion suscitee par les faits rapportes, il appelle egalement la population a continuer de faire confiance au personnel soignant de l'etablissement. a Gao, des habitants reclament des responsabilites Pres de 48 heures apres l'agression sexuelle presumee, plusieurs habitants expriment leur indignation et demandent que les responsabilites soient etablies. Pour un habitant, un tel acte dans un etablissement hospitalier pourrait reveler un defaut de surveillance. « Seule la negligence peut expliquer que quelqu'un puisse rentrer a l'hopital et commettre cet acte-la. C'est meme impensable », estime-t-il. Un autre interlocuteur insiste sur la sensibilite du lieu ou les faits se seraient produits. « Surtout a un endroit tres sensible qu'est la salle de reanimation. Je dis que c'est un acte ignoble. L'etat doit vraiment prendre des precautions », declare-t-il, appelant a renforcer les mesures de securite. L'emotion est egalement vive chez un autre habitant, qui evoque un malaise plus large face aux evenements recents dans la region. « On a le cœur serre, on a le choc. Moi, ce n'est pas l'acte, en fait, qui doit interpeller la societe. C'est une succession de fautes. C'est une succession d'evenements auxquels nous assistons ces derniers temps dans la region de Gao », deplore-t-il. Pour un chef de famille interroge sur l'affaire dans la ville de Gao, la priorite est que le suspect presume soit retrouve et traduit en justice. Une enquete pour etablir les faits Pour rappel , la patiente avait ete admise en reanimation apres une intervention chirurgicale. Elle est decedee mercredi dernier, vers 14 heures, quelques heures apres l'agression sexuelle presumee. a ce stade, aucun lien n'a ete etabli entre les faits rapportes et le deces de la patiente. L'enquete ouverte par la gendarmerie devra notamment contribuer a etablir les circonstances de l'agression presumee et a determiner les eventuelles responsabilites. Lire aussi : a Gao, la consommation de drogues inquiete les familles et les professionnels de sante L’article Gao : indignation après une agression sexuelle présumée à l’hôpital régional est apparu en premier sur Studio Tamani - Informations, débats, magazines : toute l’actualité du Mali, en 5 langues .

items.title: Kedougou : un site d’orpaillage clandestin démantelé, 25 motopompes saisies
items.description: Les forces de sécurité ont démantelé, mercredi 22 octobre 2026, un site d’orpaillage clandestin situé à cinq kilomètres du village de Tenkoto, dans la région de Kédougou. L’opération a permis la saisie de plusieurs équipements utilisés pour l’exploitation aurifère. Les éléments de la brigade de proximité de Sabodala, en poste à Tenkoto, appuyés par l’Escadron de surveillance et d’intervention (ESI) de Kédougou, ont procédé au démantèlement d’un site d’orpaillage clandestin situé à cinq kilomètres du village de Tenkoto. Menée le mercredi 22 octobre 2026, l’opération a permis aux forces de sécurité de saisir un important lot de matériel, comprenant 25 motopompes, six motocyclettes, cinq machines dites « cracheurs », deux tricycles motorisés et 70 bassines en plastique. L’enquête se poursuit afin de déterminer les circonstances de cette activité clandestine et d’identifier les personnes impliquées.
